anki_seeds.front: Contravariant functor composition law?
contravariant $\circ$ contravariant $=$ {{c1::covariant}}.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Let $G\colon\mathcal C^{op}\to\mathcal D$ and $F\colon\mathcal D^{op}\to\mathcal E$ be contravariant, so $G(g\circ f)=Gf\circ Gg$ and $F$ likewise reverses order. Then $FG(g\circ f)=F(Gf\circ Gg)=F(Gg)\circ F(Gf)=FG(g)\circ FG(f)$ — the two reversals cancel, restoring the covariant composition law. Identities are preserved by both, so $F\circ G$ is a covariant functor.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Prove that the composite of two contravariant functors is covariant.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Track the order of a composite through both functors: each contravariant step reverses it, and two reversals restore the original order. Identities survive both steps, so the composite obeys the covariant laws.

knowledge_points.constraints: State the reversed composition law $F(g\circ f)=Ff\circ Fg$ explicitly; instances are the preimage power-set or order-reversing poset maps.

exemplars.answer: A functor $\mathcal C^{op}\to\mathcal D$; preimage reverses composition.
exemplars.problem: Define a contravariant functor and verify the preimage power-set $P^{-1}\colon\mathbf{Set}^{op}\to\mathbf{Set}$, $P^{-1}(f)(T)=f^{-1}[T]$, is one.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A contravariant functor on $\mathcal C$ is a functor $\mathcal C^{op}\to\mathcal D$: it sends $f\colon A\to B$ to $Ff\colon FB\to FA$ with $F(g\circ f)=Ff\circ Fg$ and $F(1)=1$. For preimage, $(g\circ f)^{-1}[T]=f^{-1}[g^{-1}[T]]$, i.e. $P^{-1}(g\circ f)=P^{-1}(f)\circ P^{-1}(g)$, and $P^{-1}(1)=1$. So $P^{-1}$ is contravariant.

exemplars.answer: It is a functor $P^{op}\to Q$; the order-reversal is the contravariance.
exemplars.problem: Let $P,Q$ be posets viewed as categories. Show an order-reversing map $\phi\colon P\to Q$ (i.e. $x\le y$ implies $\phi(y)\le\phi(x)$) is exactly a contravariant functor $P\to Q$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: In a poset category there is a unique arrow $x\to y$ iff $x\le y$. An order-reversing $\phi$ turns $x\le y$ into $\phi(y)\le\phi(x)$, so it sends the arrow $x\to y$ to an arrow $\phi(y)\to\phi(x)$, reversing direction. Hom-sets have at most one element, so the functor laws hold automatically. Thus $\phi$ is a functor $P^{op}\to Q$, i.e. a contravariant functor $P\to Q$.

knowledge_points.name: Contravariant = functor on the opposite category

knowledge_points.constraints: Prove the variance of a composite by expanding the composition law symbolically — the two orders of reversal must be tracked step by step, never asserted.

exemplars.problem: Show that the composite of two contravariant functors is covariant.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $F,G$ be contravariant, so $G(g\circ f)=Gf\circ Gg$ and $F$ reverses order too. Then $FG(g\circ f)=F(Gf\circ Gg)=F(Gg)\circ F(Gf)=FG(g)\circ FG(f)$, which is the covariant composition law; identities are preserved, so $F\circ G$ is covariant.

exemplars.problem: If $F$ is covariant and $G$ contravariant, what is the variance of $F\circ G$?
exemplars.solution_sketch: $FG(g\circ f)=F(Gf\circ Gg)=F(Gf)\circ F(Gg)=FG(f)\circ FG(g)$, reversing order — contravariant. Covariant $\circ$ contravariant $=$ contravariant.

knowledge_points.name: Composing variances

knowledge_points.constraints: Decide variance from the direction of the morphism part AND the composition law; examples limited to duals of vector spaces, group inversion, preimage, and hom-functors.

exemplars.problem: Is the dual-space functor $V\mapsto V^*$, $f\mapsto f^*$ (precompose), covariant or contravariant on $\mathbf{Vect}$? Justify.
exemplars.solution_sketch: For $f\colon V\to W$ the dual $f^*\colon W^*\to V^*$ sends $\phi\mapsto\phi\circ f$, reversing direction. And $(g\circ f)^*(\phi)=\phi\circ g\circ f=f^*(g^*(\phi))$, so $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$. Hence $(-)^*$ is contravariant.

exemplars.problem: For a group $G$ as a one-object category $BG$, is inversion $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ a covariant or contravariant functor $BG\to BG$? Justify.
exemplars.solution_sketch: On the single object the action is forced. On morphisms, inversion fixes the identity ($e^{-1}=e$) but satisfies $(gh)^{-1}=h^{-1}g^{-1}$, reversing the order of composition. That is the contravariant law $F(gh)=F(h)\circ F(g)$, so inversion is a contravariant functor $BG\to BG$; equivalently it is the group isomorphism $G\cong G^{op}$.

knowledge_points.name: Reading off variance in examples

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the region inside the sphere $\rho \le 2$ and above the cone $\varphi \le \frac{\pi}{3}$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: $V = \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\pi/3}\!\int_0^2 \rho^2 \sin\varphi \,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta = 2\pi \cdot \tfrac{8}{3} \cdot \left[-\cos\varphi\right]_0^{\pi/3} = 2\pi \cdot \tfrac{8}{3} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{8\pi}{3}$.

knowledge_points.constraints: angles at standard unit-circle values; balls, half-balls, and cones as regions

exemplars.problem: Convert the spherical point $(\rho, \varphi, \theta) = \left(2, \frac{\pi}{3}, 0\right)$ to rectangular coordinates.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $x = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\cos 0 = \sqrt{3}$, $y = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\sin 0 = 0$, $z = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = 1$.

exemplars.problem: Describe the upper half of the unit ball in spherical coordinates.

knowledge_points.name: Spherical coordinates: conversion and set-up

knowledge_points.constraints: balls and half-balls centered at the origin; integrands are functions of rho alone or a single factor of cos(phi) (e.g. z = rho cos phi); dV = rho^2 sin(phi) d rho d phi d theta; the triple integral separates into a product of three one-variable integrals

exemplars.problem: Use spherical coordinates to verify the volume of the ball of radius $3$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi}\int_0^3 \rho^2 \sin\varphi \, d\rho\, d\varphi\, d\theta = 2\pi \cdot 2 \cdot 9 = 36\pi$ (with $\int_0^3 \rho^2 d\rho = 9$, $\int_0^\pi \sin\varphi\, d\varphi = 2$).

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\iiint_E z \, dV$ where $E$ is the upper half of the unit ball.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $z = \rho\cos\varphi$: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^1 \rho^3 \cos\varphi \sin\varphi\, d\rho\, d\varphi\, d\theta = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{4}$.

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\iiint_B e^{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}} dV$ over the unit ball.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The integrand is $e^{\rho^3}$; $\int_0^1 e^{\rho^3}\rho^2\, d\rho = \frac{e-1}{3}$ (substitute $u = \rho^3$), times $\int\sin\varphi = 2$ and $2\pi$.

knowledge_points.name: Evaluating spherical integrals

knowledge_points.constraints: 2x2 Jacobians only; cone half-angles at standard unit-circle values

exemplars.problem: Compute the Jacobian $\frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(r, \theta)}$ for the polar map $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\det\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix} = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r$ — this determinant is why $dA = r\,dr\,d\theta$.

exemplars.problem: Find the volume of the "ice-cream cone" region inside the cone $\varphi \le \frac{\pi}{3}$ and the sphere $\rho \le 1$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_0^1 \rho^2\sin\varphi\, d\rho\, d\varphi\, d\theta = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{3}\left(1 - \cos\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}$.

knowledge_points.name: Jacobians and choosing a coordinate system

diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Uniqueness of a factorization is left-cancellation in disguise: two factorizations give $m\circ u=m\circ u'$, and $m$ mono forces $u=u'$. Nothing more is needed, since the claim is only at most one, so existence is not at issue.

exemplars.problem: Let $f,p\colon A\to B$, $q,g\colon B\to D$ and $r,h\colon D\to E$ be morphisms satisfying $q\circ f=g\circ p$ and $r\circ g=h\circ q$. Chase these hypotheses to simplify $r\circ g\circ f$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The typing makes every composite below a morphism $A\to E$. Compose the second hypothesis $r\circ g=h\circ q$ on the right with $f\colon A\to B$: $r\circ g\circ f=h\circ q\circ f$. Now substitute the first hypothesis inside: $h\circ(q\circ f)=h\circ(g\circ p)$. Dropping brackets by associativity gives $r\circ g\circ f=h\circ g\circ p$. Each step only replaces a composite by an equal one, which is all a diagram chase ever does.

exemplars.solution_sketch: A monomorphism $g$ satisfies: $g\circ f=g\circ f'\Rightarrow f=f'$. That hypothesis is exactly given, so cancel $g$ on the left to get $f=f'$.

knowledge_points.constraints: Uniqueness arguments only: conclude two candidate morphisms are equal, either from a universal property's uniqueness clause or by cancelling a monomorphism; name which mechanism is used.

exemplars.problem: Two morphisms $u,v\colon X\to P$ both make the same diagram into $P$ commute, and $P$'s defining property forces at most one such map. Conclude and name the technique.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The defining (universal) property of $P$ says: for the given cone/data there is at most one morphism $X\to P$ making all triangles commute. Since $u$ and $v$ both do, uniqueness forces $u=v$. This pattern — 'exhibit a map, then use uniqueness to identify two candidates' — recurs throughout limit and adjunction proofs.

exemplars.answer: At most one such $u$; two candidates agree by cancelling the mono $m$.
exemplars.problem: Let $m\colon P\to A$ be a monomorphism. Prove that any morphism $f\colon X\to A$ factors through $m$ in at most one way: there is at most one $u\colon X\to P$ with $m\circ u=f$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Suppose $m\circ u=f=m\circ u'$ for $u,u'\colon X\to P$. Then $m\circ u=m\circ u'$, and since $m$ is a monomorphism (left-cancellable) we get $u=u'$. Hence a factorization through a mono, when it exists, is unique; here the uniqueness comes from the cancellation property rather than from a universal property.

knowledge_points.name: Uniqueness arguments via commuting constraints

exemplars.problem: A design model has volume $9x^4 - 16$ for $x>20$. Write this model as a product of integer-coefficient polynomial factors, factoring completely over the integers.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The square root of $9x^4$ is $3x^2$, while the square root of $16$ is $4$. Use $(3x^2-4)(3x^2+4)$. Neither quadratic has rational roots, so both remain integer-irreducible.

exemplars.problem: A polynomial has the following nonzero coefficients: power $2$: coefficient $16$; power $0$: coefficient $-9$. Reconstruct it and write its factored form over the integers.

exemplars.problem: Correct $(5x-2)(5x+2)$ as a factorization of $25x^4-4$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The square root of $25x^4$ is $5x^2$. Thus the factors are $5x^2-2$ and $5x^2+2$. Both quadratics have no rational roots and remain irreducible over the integers.

exemplars.problem: Factor $2x^2 - 18$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Extract the coefficient GCF $2$, leaving $x^2-9$. Its square roots are $x$ and $3$, so the complete product is $2(x-3)(x+3)$.

exemplars.problem: A design model has volume $x^4 - 16$ for $x>20$. Write this model as a product of integer-coefficient polynomial factors, factoring completely over the integers.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Write $x^4-16=(x^2-4)(x^2+4)$. Split $x^2-4$ again into $(x-2)(x+2)$; the positive sum $x^2+4$ has no real roots and stays irreducible.

exemplars.problem: A polynomial has nonzero coefficients $3$ at power $4$ and $-48$ at power $0$. Reconstruct it and factor completely over the integers.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Extract $3$ to leave $x^4-16$. Split it into $(x^2-4)(x^2+4)$, then split the first factor into $(x-2)(x+2)$. Retain the GCF and the irreducible sum of squares.

exemplars.problem: A learner stops at $(x^2-9)(x^2+9)$ when factoring $x^4-81$. Complete the factorization over the integers.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The remaining $x^2-9$ is $(x-3)(x+3)$. Keep $x^2+9$ unchanged: it has no real roots and therefore no integer linear factors.

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: In $D_5$, the symmetry group of the regular pentagon ($r$ the rotation of order $5$, $s$ a reflection), how many elements have order $2$?
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Each of the five reflections $r^{k}s$ squares to the identity: $(r^{k}s)(r^{k}s) = r^{k}(sr^{k}s) = r^{k}r^{-k} = e$. A rotation $r^{k}$ has order $2$ only if $5 \mid 2k$, impossible for $1 \le k \le 4$. So exactly the $5$ reflections.

diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: $\mathcal{L}\{\delta(t)\} = 1$, so $H(s) = \frac{1}{s^2 + 4s + 3} = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s+3)} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{s+1} - \frac{1}{s+3}\right)$.

exemplars.problem: Compute $\int_0^5 \delta(t - 3)(t^2 + 1)\,dt$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The impulse at $t = 3$ lies inside $(0, 5)$, so the integral is $3^2 + 1$.

exemplars.problem: Solve $y' + 2y = \delta(t - 1)$, $y(0) = 0$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $(s + 2)Y = e^{-s}$, so $Y = \frac{e^{-s}}{s+2}$; invert with the second shifting theorem.

exemplars.problem: Solve $y'' + y = \delta(t - \pi)$, $y(0) = y'(0) = 0$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $Y = \frac{e^{-\pi s}}{s^2 + 1}$; the delayed inverse of $\frac{1}{s^2+1}$ is $u_{\pi}(t)\sin(t - \pi)$.

exemplars.problem: A resting system obeys $y'' + 4y = \delta(t)$, $y(0) = y'(0) = 0$. Find the response.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $Y = \frac{1}{s^2 + 4}$ inverts straight from the table.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Converges: for $n \ge 2$, $n^2 - n \ge \frac{n^2}{2}$, so $\frac{1}{n^2-n} \le \frac{2}{n^2}$, and $\sum \frac{2}{n^2}$ is a convergent $p$-series

diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: A comparison that bounds the terms from below by a convergent series proves nothing; halving the denominator restores a usable upper bound.

exemplars.problem: Decide whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2 + 3}$ converges, with justification.

exemplars.problem: Decide whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^n + 1}$ converges.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\frac{1}{2^n + 1} < \frac{1}{2^n}$ and $\sum 2^{-n}$ converges.

exemplars.problem: Decide whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\sin^2 n}{n^2}$ converges.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $0 \le \sin^2 n \le 1$ bounds the terms by a convergent $p$-series.

exemplars.problem: Decide whether $\sum_{n=3}^{\infty} \frac{\ln n}{n}$ converges.

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: What is the largest order of an element of $\mathbb{Z}_6 \times \mathbb{Z}_{10}$?
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: The order of $(a,b)$ is $\mathrm{lcm}(|a|,|b|)$, and the largest orders available in the factors are $6$ and $10$, so the maximum is $\mathrm{lcm}(6,10) = 30$, attained by $(1,1)$. Since $30 < 60$, the group is not cyclic.

knowledge_points.constraints: 2-3 factors, each Z_n with n <= 12; componentwise arithmetic

exemplars.problem: In $\mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_6$, compute $(3, 5) + (2, 4)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Add componentwise: $3+2 = 5 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $5+4 = 9 \equiv 3 \pmod 6$.

exemplars.problem: What is the order of the group $\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_5 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$?
exemplars.solution_sketch: $|A \times B| = |A||B|$; $3 \cdot 5 \cdot 2 = 30$.

exemplars.problem: Find the order of $(2, 3)$ in $\mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_6$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $|2|$ in $\mathbb{Z}_4$ is $2$; $|3|$ in $\mathbb{Z}_6$ is $2$; the order of the pair is $\mathrm{lcm}(2,2) = 2$.

exemplars.problem: How many elements of order $12$ does $\mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_6$ contain?
exemplars.solution_sketch: Need $\mathrm{lcm}(|a|, |b|) = 12$: $|a| = 4$ ($2$ choices) and $|b| \in \{3, 6\}$ ($2 + 2 = 4$ choices), giving $2 \cdot 4 = 8$.

exemplars.problem: The product $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_3$ is cyclic, so it is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Give $n$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\mathbb{Z}_m \times \mathbb{Z}_n$ is cyclic iff $\gcd(m,n) = 1$, and then it is $\mathbb{Z}_{mn}$: here $\gcd(2,3) = 1$, so the product is $\mathbb{Z}_6$. By contrast $\mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_6$ is not cyclic, since its maximum element order is $\mathrm{lcm}(4,6) = 12 < 24$.

exemplars.problem: What is the largest order of an element of $\mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_6$?
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\mathrm{lcm}$ of component orders is maximized at $\mathrm{lcm}(4, 6) = 12$, e.g. by $(1,1)$.

anki_seeds.front: Definitions of even and odd integers?

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Suppose $a \mid b$, so $b = ak$ for some integer $k$. Then $3b^2 + b = 3(ak)^2 + ak = a(3ak^2 + k)$, and $3ak^2 + k$ is an integer, so $a \mid (3b^2 + b)$ by the definition of divisibility.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Prove: for all integers $a, b$, if $a \mid b$ then $a \mid (3b^2 + b)$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Unfold the divisibility hypothesis as $b = ak$, substitute, and factor $a$ out of the result.

knowledge_points.constraints: assume the hypothesis and derive the conclusion; use even = $2k$, odd = $2k+1$

exemplars.answer: Direct: write $m = 2a$, $n = 2b$; then $m + n = 2(a + b)$, even.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for all integers $m, n$, if $m$ and $n$ are even then $m + n$ is even.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Assume $m, n$ are even, so $m = 2a$ and $n = 2b$ for integers $a, b$. Then $m + n = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$, and $a + b \in \mathbb{Z}$, so $m + n$ is even. $\square$

exemplars.problem: Prove: the product of two odd integers is odd.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $m = 2a + 1$ and $n = 2b + 1$. Then $mn = 4ab + 2a + 2b + 1 = 2(2ab + a + b) + 1$, and $2ab + a + b \in \mathbb{Z}$, so $mn$ is odd. $\square$

exemplars.answer: $n^2 + n = n(n+1)$ is a product of consecutive integers, one of which is even.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for every integer $n$, $n^2 + n$ is even.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $n^2 + n = n(n + 1)$. Of two consecutive integers $n$ and $n + 1$, one is even, so the product is even. $\square$

exemplars.answer: From $b - a \ge 0$ and $c \ge 0$, $(b - a)c \ge 0$, so $ac \le bc$.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for real numbers, if $a \le b$ and $c \ge 0$ then $ac \le bc$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Assume $a \le b$, so $b - a \ge 0$. With $c \ge 0$, the product $(b - a)c \ge 0$, i.e. $bc - ac \ge 0$, hence $ac \le bc$. $\square$

exemplars.answer: $b = ak$, $c = bm$ give $c = a(km)$, so $a \mid c$.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for all integers $a, b, c$, if $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$ then $a \mid c$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Assume $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$, so $b = ak$ and $c = bm$ for integers $k, m$. Then $c = (ak)m = a(km)$ with $km \in \mathbb{Z}$, so $a \mid c$. $\square$

exemplars.problem: Prove: for all integers $n$, if $5 \mid n$ then $5 \mid n^2$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Assume $5 \mid n$, so $n = 5k$. Then $n^2 = 25k^2 = 5(5k^2)$ with $5k^2 \in \mathbb{Z}$, so $5 \mid n^2$. $\square$

anki_seeds.back: only the identities $1_x$ — one for each $x\in S$.
anki_seeds.front: The discrete category on a set $S$ has which morphisms?

anki_seeds.back: exactly one for every ordered pair (so $|S|^2$ in total); it is a groupoid.
anki_seeds.front: The indiscrete category on $S$ has how many morphisms $x\to y$?
A functor $\mathbf{2}=(0\to 1)\to\mathcal{C}$ is the same thing as {{c1::a morphism of $\mathcal{C}$}}.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Let $u\colon x\to y$ be the unique arrow and $v\colon y\to x$ the unique arrow back. Then $v\circ u$ is an arrow $x\to x$; since $\mathrm{Hom}(x,x)$ has exactly one element, which must be $1_x$, we get $v\circ u=1_x$. Likewise $u\circ v=1_y$. So $u$ has a two-sided inverse and is an isomorphism.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: In the indiscrete category $\mathrm{indisc}(S)$ (exactly one arrow between each ordered pair of objects of $S$), prove that every morphism is an isomorphism.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: The whole argument is a counting step: $\mathrm{Hom}(x,x)$ has exactly one element and $1_x$ lies in it, so any arrow $x\to x$ — in particular each round trip $v\circ u$ and $u\circ v$ — must be an identity.

knowledge_points.constraints: Work with an arbitrary set $S$ and give morphism counts as a formula in $|S|$ (identities included); any concrete instance uses a set of size at most 4.

exemplars.answer: Objects $S$, morphisms only the identities; it has exactly $|S|$ morphisms.
exemplars.problem: Define the discrete category $\mathrm{disc}(S)$ on a set $S$, verify it is a category, and count its morphisms.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Take the objects to be the elements of $S$, with $\mathrm{Hom}(x,x)=\{1_x\}$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(x,y)=\varnothing$ for $x\neq y$. The only composable pairs are $1_x\circ 1_x=1_x$, so composition is total, associative and unital: $\mathrm{disc}(S)$ is a category. Its morphisms are exactly the $|S|$ identities. As a preorder it is the equality relation, and every morphism is invertible, so it is also a groupoid.

exemplars.answer: The object part is an arbitrary family $(C_x)_{x\in S}$; the morphism part is forced to send $1_x\mapsto 1_{C_x}$.
exemplars.problem: Show that a functor $\mathrm{disc}(S)\to\mathcal{C}$ is the same thing as an $S$-indexed family of objects of $\mathcal{C}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A functor $D$ assigns an object $Dx$ to each $x\in S$, and to each morphism a morphism. The only morphisms of $\mathrm{disc}(S)$ are the identities, and functoriality forces $D(1_x)=1_{Dx}$, so the morphism part carries no information and the functor laws impose no condition. Hence functors $\mathrm{disc}(S)\to\mathcal{C}$ correspond bijectively to families $(Dx)_{x\in S}$ of objects — this is why a diagram of discrete shape is just a family of objects.

knowledge_points.name: The discrete category on a set

knowledge_points.constraints: Work with an arbitrary set $S$, giving counts as a formula in $|S|$; justify uniqueness of each arrow before composing, and any concrete instance uses a set of size at most 4.

exemplars.answer: Objects $S$, one arrow for each ordered pair; it has $|S|^2$ morphisms.
exemplars.problem: Define the indiscrete category $\mathrm{indisc}(S)$ (exactly one morphism between each ordered pair of objects), verify it is a category, and count its morphisms.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Set $\mathrm{Hom}(x,y)=\{*\}$ for all $x,y\in S$. Composition is forced (there is only one candidate arrow $x\to z$), and associativity and the unit laws hold automatically because each hom-set has one element; the unique arrow $x\to x$ must be $1_x$. So $\mathrm{indisc}(S)$ is a category with one morphism per ordered pair, i.e. $|S|^2$ morphisms in total.

exemplars.answer: Every arrow is invertible; the preorder is the total relation $x\le y$ for all $x,y$.
exemplars.problem: Prove that $\mathrm{indisc}(S)$ is a groupoid, and identify the preorder it corresponds to.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $u\colon x\to y$ and $v\colon y\to x$ be the unique arrows. Then $v\circ u\colon x\to x$ and $u\circ v\colon y\to y$ are the unique arrows there, namely $1_x$ and $1_y$. So $u$ is an isomorphism and $\mathrm{indisc}(S)$ is a groupoid. It is thin, and its associated preorder has $x\le y$ for every pair — the total preorder, in which all objects are isomorphic.

knowledge_points.name: The indiscrete category

knowledge_points.constraints: Shape categories with at most three objects; state the functor's data explicitly.

exemplars.answer: No data at all; a single object; a single morphism of $\mathcal{C}$.
exemplars.problem: Describe what a functor $\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$ is for each shape $\mathcal{J}=\mathbf{0}$ (empty), $\mathbf{1}$ (one object), and $\mathbf{2}=(0\to 1)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: For $\mathbf{0}$ there are no objects or morphisms to send anywhere, so there is exactly one functor $\mathbf{0}\to\mathcal{C}$ and it carries no data — the empty diagram. For $\mathbf{1}$ (one object and its identity) a functor is determined by the image object, since the identity must go to an identity. For $\mathbf{2}$, a functor picks objects $F0,F1$ and a morphism $F0\to F1$, with identities forced; so a functor $\mathbf{2}\to\mathcal{C}$ is exactly an arrow of $\mathcal{C}$.

exemplars.answer: A parallel pair $f,g\colon A\to B$ in $\mathcal{C}$; a pair of morphisms $A\to C\leftarrow B$ with common codomain.
exemplars.problem: Describe a functor out of the parallel-pair shape ($\bullet\rightrightarrows\bullet$) and out of the cospan shape ($\bullet\to\bullet\leftarrow\bullet$).
exemplars.solution_sketch: The parallel-pair shape has objects $0,1$ and two distinct non-identity arrows $0\rightrightarrows 1$ (there are no other composites to specify), so a functor to $\mathcal{C}$ chooses objects $A=F0$, $B=F1$ and two morphisms $f,g\colon A\to B$. The cospan shape has three objects $0,2,1$ with arrows $0\to 2\leftarrow 1$, so a functor chooses $A\to C\leftarrow B$. These are exactly the shapes whose universal cones are the equalizer and the pullback.

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Find the upward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle y,\; -x,\; z \rangle$ through the paraboloid $z = 4 - x^2 - y^2$, $z \ge 0$, by closing the surface with the disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 4$ in the plane $z = 0$ and applying the divergence theorem.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = 1$, so the total outward flux through the closed surface equals the volume $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^2 (4 - r^2)\,r\,dr\,d\theta = 8\pi$. On the bottom disk the outward normal is $\langle 0,0,-1\rangle$ and $\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{n} = -z = 0$, so the whole $8\pi$ passes upward through the paraboloid.

exemplars.problem: Use the divergence theorem to find the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle x^2, y^2, z^2 \rangle$ through the boundary of the unit cube $[0,1]^3$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = 2x + 2y + 2z$; $\iiint_{[0,1]^3} (2x + 2y + 2z)\, dV = 3 \cdot 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 3$.

exemplars.problem: Use the divergence theorem to find the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle x, y, z^2 \rangle$ through the closed cylinder $x^2 + y^2 \le 1$, $0 \le z \le 1$, and check it against the piece-by-piece surface computation, which gives $3\pi$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = 2 + 2z$; slicing the cylinder, $\iiint (2 + 2z)\, dV = \pi \int_0^1 (2 + 2z)\, dz = \pi(2 + 1) = 3\pi$ — agreeing with the lateral-plus-caps computation.

exemplars.problem: Use the divergence theorem to find the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle x^3, y^3, z^3 \rangle$ through the unit sphere.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = 3(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) = 3\rho^2$; in spherical coordinates $\iiint 3\rho^2 \cdot \rho^2 \sin\varphi\, d\rho\, d\varphi\, d\theta = 4\pi \cdot 3 \cdot \frac{1}{5} = \frac{12\pi}{5}$.

exemplars.problem: Use the divergence theorem to find the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle xy^2, yz^2, zx^2 \rangle$ through the unit sphere.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = y^2 + z^2 + x^2 = \rho^2$; $\iiint_B \rho^2\, dV = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1 \rho^4 \sin\varphi\, d\rho\, d\varphi\, d\theta = 2\pi \cdot 2 \cdot \frac{1}{5} = \frac{4\pi}{5}$.

On the bottom disk the outward normal is $\langle 0, 0, -1 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} = -z = 0$, so the paraboloid carries all of it: $\frac{\pi}{2}$ — matching the direct parametrized computation.

exemplars.problem: What is the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle y, z, x \rangle$ through the sphere of radius $3$? Justify without computing any surface integral.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0$, so by the divergence theorem the flux through any closed surface is $\iiint 0\, dV = 0$.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Write $m = 2a + 1$ and $n = 2b + 1$ with $a, b$ integers. Then $m^2 + n^2 - 2 = (4a^2 + 4a + 1) + (4b^2 + 4b + 1) - 2 = 4(a^2 + a + b^2 + b)$. Since $a^2 + a + b^2 + b$ is an integer, $4 \mid (m^2 + n^2 - 2)$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Prove: for all integers $m, n$, if $m$ and $n$ are both odd then $4 \mid (m^2 + n^2 - 2)$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Substitute the odd forms, expand both squares, and factor $4$ out of what remains.

knowledge_points.constraints: prove divisibility of linear combinations from the definition of divides

exemplars.answer: $b = ak$, $c = al$ give $bx + cy = a(kx + ly)$.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for all integers $a, b, c, x, y$, if $a \mid b$ and $a \mid c$ then $a \mid (bx + cy)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Write $b = ak$ and $c = al$. Then $bx + cy = akx + aly = a(kx + ly)$ with $kx + ly \in \mathbb{Z}$, so $a \mid (bx + cy)$; taking $x = y = 1$ gives $a \mid (b + c)$. $\square$

exemplars.problem: Prove: for all integers $a, b$, if $a \mid b$ then $a \mid b^2$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Write $b = ak$. Then $b^2 = a^2 k^2 = a(a k^2)$ with $a k^2 \in \mathbb{Z}$, so $a \mid b^2$. $\square$

knowledge_points.constraints: argue from the two parity forms of an integer

exemplars.answer: If $n = 2k$ then $n + 1$ is odd; if $n = 2k + 1$ then $n + 1$ is even.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for every integer $n$, exactly one of $n$ and $n + 1$ is even.
exemplars.solution_sketch: If $n = 2k$ (even) then $n + 1 = 2k + 1$ is odd; if $n = 2k + 1$ (odd) then $n + 1 = 2(k + 1)$ is even. In each situation exactly one is even. $\square$

exemplars.problem: Prove: the sum of an even integer and an odd integer is odd.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let the even integer be $2a$ and the odd one $2b + 1$. Their sum is $2a + 2b + 1 = 2(a + b) + 1$, which is odd. $\square$

knowledge_points.name: Parity arguments

knowledge_points.constraints: iff proof; handle both directions

exemplars.answer: $n$ even gives $n^2$ even; contrapositive gives the converse.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for every integer $n$, $n^2$ is even if and only if $n$ is even.
exemplars.solution_sketch: If $n = 2k$ then $n^2 = 2(2k^2)$ is even. Conversely, if $n$ is odd, $n = 2k + 1$ gives $n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$, odd; contrapositively, $n^2$ even forces $n$ even. $\square$

exemplars.answer: $n$ odd gives $n^2$ odd; contrapositive gives the converse.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for every integer $n$, $n^2$ is odd if and only if $n$ is odd.
exemplars.solution_sketch: If $n = 2k + 1$ then $n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$ is odd. Conversely, if $n$ is even, $n = 2k$ gives $n^2 = 2(2k^2)$ even; contrapositively, $n^2$ odd forces $n$ odd. $\square$

knowledge_points.name: Parity of squares and products

diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = -15 < 0$ (obtuse); $\cos\theta = -15/(3\sqrt2 \cdot 5) = -1/\sqrt2$, so $\theta = 135^\circ$.

exemplars.solution_sketch: $(4)(1) + (-2)(2) = 4 - 4 = 0$; zero dot product means orthogonal.

exemplars.solution_sketch: $6 - 6k = 0$ forces $k = 1$.

exemplars.problem: Is the angle between $(2, 1)$ and $(1, -3)$ acute, right, or obtuse?

exemplars.problem: Is the angle between $(3, 1)$ and $(1, 2)$ acute, right, or obtuse?
exemplars.solution_sketch: Dot product $3 + 2 = 5 > 0$.

exemplars.problem: Find all $k$ so that the angle between $(1, 0)$ and $(1, k)$ is $60^\circ$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + k^2}} = \frac{1}{2}$ gives $k^2 = 3$.

exemplars.solution_sketch: $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{1 \cdot \sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $\theta = 45^\circ$.

exemplars.problem: Find the angle between $(2, 2)$ and $(0, 3)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\cos\theta = \frac{6}{2\sqrt{2} \cdot 3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

exemplars.problem: Find $\cos\theta$ for the angle $\theta$ between $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\cos\theta = \frac{2 + 2}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5}} = \frac{4}{5}$.

exemplars.problem: Given $\|\mathbf{u}\| = 3$, $\|\mathbf{v}\| = 4$, and $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$, find $\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|$.
Given $\|\mathbf{u}\| = 2$, $\|\mathbf{v}\| = 1$, and $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 1$, compute $\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|^2$.
If $\|\mathbf{u}\| = \|\mathbf{v}\|$, show that $(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) \cdot (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}) = 0$.

exemplars.solution_sketch: $|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| = 4$; $\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{5}\sqrt{5} = 5$.

anki_seeds.front: Center of mass formulas for a lamina with density $\rho$?

anki_seeds.back: The center of mass with constant density — the geometric center $\left(\frac{1}{A}\iint x\, dA, \frac{1}{A}\iint y\, dA\right)$.
anki_seeds.front: What is the centroid of a region?

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Find the centre of mass of the lamina occupying $[0, 2] \times [0, 1]$ with density $\rho(x, y) = x$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: $m = \int_0^2\!\int_0^1 x\,dy\,dx = 2$; $M_y = \int_0^2\!\int_0^1 x^2\,dy\,dx = \tfrac{8}{3}$; $M_x = \int_0^2\!\int_0^1 xy\,dy\,dx = 1$. Hence $\bar x = \tfrac{8}{3}/2 = \tfrac{4}{3}$ and $\bar y = 1/2$.

knowledge_points.constraints: density polynomial of degree at most 2; rectangles or triangles with integer vertices; masses exact rationals

exemplars.problem: Find the mass of the lamina occupying $[0,1] \times [0,1]$ with density $\rho(x, y) = x + y$.
Find the mass of the triangular lamina with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$ and density $\rho(x, y) = 2xy$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $m = \int_0^1 \int_0^x 2xy\, dy\, dx = \int_0^1 x \cdot x^2\, dx = \frac{1}{4}$.

knowledge_points.name: Mass of a lamina

knowledge_points.constraints: M_y integrates x*rho, M_x integrates y*rho; rectangles only; answers exact rationals

exemplars.problem: For the uniform lamina ($\rho = 1$) on $[0,2] \times [0,1]$, compute the moments $M_y = \iint x\, dA$ and $M_x = \iint y\, dA$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $M_y = \int_0^2 x\, dx \cdot 1 = 2$; $M_x = 2 \cdot \int_0^1 y\, dy = 1$.

exemplars.problem: For the lamina on $[0,1]^2$ with density $\rho = y$, compute the moment $M_x = \iint y \rho \, dA$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $M_x = \iint y^2\, dA = \int_0^1 y^2\, dy = \frac{1}{3}$.

knowledge_points.name: Moments about the axes

knowledge_points.constraints: use symmetry when available; centroids/centers have small rational coordinates

exemplars.problem: Find the centroid of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Area $\frac{1}{2}$; $\bar{x} = 2\int_0^1 x \cdot x\, dx = \frac{2}{3}$, $\bar{y} = 2\int_0^1 \frac{x^2}{2}\, dx = \frac{1}{3}$ (the average of the vertices).

exemplars.problem: Find the centroid of the region under $y = 4 - x^2$ and above the $x$-axis.
Find the center of mass of the lamina on $[0,1]^2$ with density $\rho(x, y) = y$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $m = \frac{1}{2}$; $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{m}\iint x y\, dA = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$; $\bar{y} = \frac{1}{m}\iint y^2\, dA = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}$.

knowledge_points.name: Center of mass and centroids

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Evaluate $\int_0^1 \int_{3y}^{3} e^{x^2}\,dx\,dy$ by reversing the order of integration.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: The region $0 \le y \le 1$, $3y \le x \le 3$ is the triangle $0 \le x \le 3$, $0 \le y \le x/3$. Reversed: $\int_0^3 \int_0^{x/3} e^{x^2}\,dy\,dx = \int_0^3 \frac{x}{3}e^{x^2}\,dx = \frac{1}{6}\left[e^{x^2}\right]_0^3 = \frac{e^9 - 1}{6}$.

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\iint_D x \, dA$ where $D$ is bounded by $y = x^2$ and $y = x$.
Evaluate $\iint_D xy \, dA$ where $D$ is the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Type I: $0 \le x \le 1$, $0 \le y \le x$: $\int_0^1 x \cdot \frac{x^2}{2}\, dx = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{8}$.

Evaluate $\iint_D (2x + y) \, dA$ where $D$ is bounded by $y = x^2$ and $y = 4$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\int_{-2}^2 \int_{x^2}^4 (2x + y)\, dy\, dx$: the $2x$ part integrates to zero by symmetry, leaving $\int_{-2}^2 \frac{16 - x^4}{2}\, dx = 32 - \frac{32}{5} = \frac{128}{5}$.

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\int_0^1 \int_y^1 e^{x^2} \, dx \, dy$ by reversing the order of integration.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The region is $0 \le y \le x \le 1$; reversed: $\int_0^1 \int_0^x e^{x^2}\, dy\, dx = \int_0^1 x e^{x^2}\, dx = \frac{e-1}{2}$.

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\int_0^1 \int_x^1 \sin(y^2) \, dy \, dx$ by reversing the order of integration.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Region $0 \le x \le y \le 1$; reversed: $\int_0^1 y \sin(y^2)\, dy = \left[-\frac{\cos(y^2)}{2}\right]_0^1$.

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Find the volume of the solid lying under the paraboloid $z = 16 - x^2 - y^2$ and above the $xy$-plane.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: The paraboloid meets $z = 0$ on the circle $r = 4$, so $V = \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^4 (16 - r^2)\,r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\left[8r^2 - \tfrac{r^4}{4}\right]_0^4 = 2\pi(128 - 64) = 128\pi$.

knowledge_points.constraints: integrands are functions of x^2+y^2; disks or annuli centered at the origin; radii small integers

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\iint_D (x^2 + y^2)\, dA$ where $D$ is the disk $x^2 + y^2 \le 4$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^2 r^2 \cdot r \, dr\, d\theta = 2\pi \left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = 2\pi \cdot 4 = 8\pi$.

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\iint_D e^{-x^2 - y^2}\, dA$ where $D$ is the unit disk.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^1 e^{-r^2} r \, dr\, d\theta = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1 - e^{-1}}{2}$; the extra $r$ makes the substitution $u = r^2$ work.

knowledge_points.name: Converting and evaluating over disks

knowledge_points.constraints: cardioids/circles for area; paraboloid caps for volume; answers exact multiples of pi

exemplars.problem: Find the area enclosed by the cardioid $r = 2 + 2\sin\theta$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi} (2 + 2\sin\theta)^2\, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi} \left(4 + 8\sin\theta + 4\sin^2\theta\right) d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left(8\pi + 0 + 4\pi\right) = 6\pi$, using $\int_0^{2\pi} \sin^2\theta\, d\theta = \pi$.

exemplars.problem: Find the volume of the solid under $z = 4 - x^2 - y^2$ and above the $xy$-plane.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The paraboloid meets $z = 0$ at $r = 2$: $\int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^2 (4 - r^2) r \, dr\, d\theta = 2\pi\left[2r^2 - \frac{r^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = 2\pi(8 - 4) = 8\pi$.

knowledge_points.name: Areas and volumes via polar

anki_seeds.back: the same objects, morphisms $A\to B$ = $\mathcal{C}$-morphisms $B\to A$, and reversed composition.
anki_seeds.front: The opposite category $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ has...
By duality: the dual of a monomorphism is an {{c1::epimorphism}}, of an initial object a {{c2::terminal object}}, of a product a {{c3::coproduct}}.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: A morphism is epi in $\mathcal C$ iff it is mono in $\mathcal C^{op}$ (reversing arrows turns right-cancellation into left-cancellation), and the composite $g\circ f$ in $\mathcal C$ is the composite $f\circ^{op}g$ in $\mathcal C^{op}$. Let $f,g$ be epis in $\mathcal C$; they are monos in $\mathcal C^{op}$, and the mono theorem, valid in every category, applies to $\mathcal C^{op}$: their composite is mono there. Translating back, $g\circ f$ is epi in $\mathcal C$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: You know that a composite of two monomorphisms is a monomorphism. Using duality — not a fresh cancellation argument — prove that a composite of two epimorphisms is an epimorphism.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Do not re-run the cancellation argument. Translate instead: epi in $\mathcal C$ is mono in $\mathcal C^{op}$ and composition order reverses, so apply the mono theorem inside $\mathcal C^{op}$, where it holds because it holds in every category, and translate the conclusion back.

knowledge_points.constraints: Define $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ precisely (hom-sets, reversed composition, identities) and verify the axioms; concrete readings only in $\mathbf{Set}$.

exemplars.problem: Given a category $\mathcal{C}$, define $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ and verify it is a category.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ has the same objects, and a morphism $A\to B$ in $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ is a morphism $B\to A$ in $\mathcal{C}$. Define $g\circ^{op} f := f\circ g$. Identities are unchanged. Associativity in $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ is associativity in $\mathcal{C}$ read backwards, and the unit laws are preserved, so $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ is a category, and $(\mathcal{C}^{op})^{op}=\mathcal{C}$.

exemplars.problem: What is $\mathbf{Set}^{op}$-morphism $A\to B$ concretely?
exemplars.solution_sketch: By definition arrows reverse, so a morphism $A\to B$ in $\mathbf{Set}^{op}$ is exactly a function $B\to A$.

knowledge_points.name: The opposite category

knowledge_points.constraints: Produce the dual of a given notion by systematically reversing arrows and justify the translation; dual pairs limited to mono/epi, initial/terminal, product/coproduct, section/retraction.

exemplars.answer: Any theorem yields its dual by reversing arrows; the dual of mono is epi.
exemplars.problem: Explain the duality principle and use it to derive the notion dual to a monomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A statement holds in all categories iff its arrow-reversed statement holds in all categories (apply the original to $\mathcal{C}^{op}$). A monomorphism in $\mathcal{C}$ is a morphism that is left-cancellable; reversing all arrows turns left-cancellation into right-cancellation, i.e. an epimorphism. So 'epi' is dual to 'mono', and every theorem about monos has a mirror theorem about epis obtained by reversing arrows.

exemplars.problem: What is the dual notion of an initial object, and why?
exemplars.solution_sketch: Initial means 'unique arrow out to every object'; reversing arrows gives 'unique arrow in from every object', which is terminal. Thus terminal is dual to initial, so any theorem about initial objects dualizes to one about terminal objects (e.g. uniqueness up to unique iso).

knowledge_points.name: The duality principle

knowledge_points.constraints: The proof must consist of applying a known theorem in $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ and translating back — no fresh diagram chase or cancellation argument allowed.

exemplars.answer: Terminal in $\mathcal{C}$ = initial in $\mathcal{C}^{op}$, so the theorem transfers.
exemplars.problem: You proved initial objects are unique up to unique iso. Explain, using duality, why no separate proof is needed for terminal objects.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A terminal object of $\mathcal{C}$ is precisely an initial object of $\mathcal{C}^{op}$. The statement 'initial objects are unique up to unique isomorphism' holds in every category, in particular in $\mathcal{C}^{op}$; translating back, terminal objects of $\mathcal{C}$ are unique up to unique isomorphism. Duality gives the theorem for free.

exemplars.answer: Applying the mono result in $\mathcal{C}^{op}$ gives: a composite of two epimorphisms is an epimorphism.
exemplars.problem: Earlier you proved that a composite of two monomorphisms is a monomorphism. Use duality to obtain the corresponding fact for epimorphisms with no new computation.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Epimorphisms in $\mathcal{C}$ are exactly monomorphisms in $\mathcal{C}^{op}$, and a composite $g\circ f$ in $\mathcal{C}$ is the composite $f\circ^{op} g$ in $\mathcal{C}^{op}$. The theorem 'a composite of two monos is a mono' holds in every category, in particular $\mathcal{C}^{op}$; read back in $\mathcal{C}$ it says a composite of two epis is an epi. No fresh cancellation argument is needed.

knowledge_points.name: Using duality to halve the work

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: For $x\in X$ pick $a\in A$ with $e(a)=x$ (possible: $e$ is surjective) and set $d(x)=u(a)$. Well defined: if $e(a)=e(a')$ then $m(u(a))=v(e(a))=v(e(a'))=m(u(a'))$, and $m$ injective gives $u(a)=u(a')$. By construction $d\circ e=u$, and $m(d(x))=m(u(a))=v(e(a))=v(x)$, so $m\circ d=v$. Uniqueness: if $m\circ d=v=m\circ d'$ then injectivity of $m$ forces $d=d'$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: In $\mathbf{Set}$, suppose $v\circ e=m\circ u$ with $e\colon A\to X$ surjective and $m\colon Y\to B$ injective. Construct a diagonal $d\colon X\to Y$ with $d\circ e=u$ and $m\circ d=v$, and prove it is the only one.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Define $d$ by choosing a preimage under the surjection $e$; the real work is showing the choice does not matter, and that is where injectivity of $m$ is spent. Uniqueness of $d$ then follows from injectivity of $m$ again.

exemplars.answer: $f=m\circ e$ with $e\colon A\twoheadrightarrow f[A]$ and $m\colon f[A]\hookrightarrow B$; any other such factorization differs by a unique bijection.
exemplars.problem: Show every function $f\colon A\to B$ factors as a surjection followed by an injection, and prove the factorization is unique up to a unique isomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $I=f[A]$, let $e(a)=f(a)$ (surjective onto $I$) and let $m$ be the inclusion $I\hookrightarrow B$; then $m\circ e=f$. Suppose also $f=m'\circ e'$ with $e'\colon A\twoheadrightarrow I'$ surjective and $m'\colon I'\hookrightarrow B$ injective. Then $m'[I']=m'[e'[A]]=f[A]=I$, so $m'$ corestricts to a bijection $\varphi\colon I'\to I$ with $m\circ\varphi=m'$. Also $m\circ\varphi\circ e'=m'\circ e'=f=m\circ e$, and $m$ is injective, so $\varphi\circ e'=e$. Finally $\varphi$ is unique: any $\psi$ with $m\circ\psi=m'$ satisfies $\psi=\varphi$ because $m$ is monic.

exemplars.answer: $A\twoheadrightarrow\{a,c\}\hookrightarrow\{a,b,c\}$; the image is $\{a,c\}$ and $b$ is not hit.
exemplars.problem: Compute the image factorization of $f\colon\{1,2,3,4\}\to\{a,b,c\}$ given by $f(1)=a$, $f(2)=a$, $f(3)=c$, $f(4)=c$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The image is $f[A]=\{a,c\}$. The surjective part $e\colon\{1,2,3,4\}\to\{a,c\}$ sends $1,2\mapsto a$ and $3,4\mapsto c$; the injective part is the inclusion $\{a,c\}\hookrightarrow\{a,b,c\}$. Their composite is $f$, and $e$ is surjective while the inclusion is injective, as required.

knowledge_points.name: The image factorization in Set

knowledge_points.constraints: State which of 'epi' and 'mono' is used at each step; uniqueness must come from the mono.

exemplars.answer: Two candidates agree because $m$ is left-cancellable.
exemplars.problem: Suppose $v\circ e=m\circ u$ with $e\colon A\to X$ epi and $m\colon Y\to B$ mono. Prove that a diagonal $d\colon X\to Y$ with $d\circ e=u$ and $m\circ d=v$ is unique if it exists.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $d,d'$ both satisfy the two equations. From $m\circ d=v=m\circ d'$ and $m$ monic (left-cancellable) we get $d=d'$. (The epi $e$ is not needed for uniqueness; it is what makes existence plausible, since $d$ is forced on the image of $e$.) Unique diagonal fill-in is only one of the axioms: a pair $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{M})$ of classes of morphisms is a factorization system when (i) every morphism factors as $m\circ e$ with $e\in\mathcal{E}$ and $m\in\mathcal{M}$, (ii) each class contains all isomorphisms and is closed under composition with them, and (iii) every commuting square $v\circ e=m\circ u$ with $e\in\mathcal{E}$, $m\in\mathcal{M}$ has a unique diagonal fill-in. Axiom (iii) alone would be satisfied vacuously by empty classes.

exemplars.answer: $d(x)=u(a)$ for any $a$ with $e(a)=x$; this is well defined and satisfies both equations.
exemplars.problem: Prove that in $\mathbf{Set}$ the diagonal fill-in always exists: given $v\circ e=m\circ u$ with $e$ surjective and $m$ injective, construct $d$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Given $x\in X$, pick $a\in A$ with $e(a)=x$ (possible as $e$ is surjective) and set $d(x)=u(a)$. Well defined: if $e(a)=e(a')=x$ then $m(u(a))=v(e(a))=v(x)=v(e(a'))=m(u(a'))$, and $m$ injective gives $u(a)=u(a')$. By construction $d\circ e=u$, and $m(d(x))=m(u(a))=v(e(a))=v(x)$, so $m\circ d=v$. Uniqueness was shown above, so $(\text{surjections},\text{injections})$ is a factorization system on $\mathbf{Set}$.

knowledge_points.name: The diagonal fill-in

knowledge_points.constraints: Order monos by factorization; every comparison map must be justified as unique.

exemplars.answer: Reflexive via $1$, transitive by composing the comparison maps; mutual factorization gives mutually inverse $t,t'$.
exemplars.problem: For monomorphisms $m\colon S\to B$ and $m'\colon S'\to B$, define $m\le m'$ to mean $m=m'\circ t$ for some $t$. Prove $\le$ is a preorder and that $m\le m'\le m$ forces $t$ to be an isomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Reflexivity: $m=m\circ 1_S$. Transitivity: if $m=m'\circ t$ and $m'=m''\circ s$ then $m=m''\circ(s\circ t)$. The factoring map is unique, since $m'\circ t=m'\circ \tilde t$ and $m'$ monic give $t=\tilde t$. Now suppose $m=m'\circ t$ and $m'=m\circ t'$. Then $m=m\circ t'\circ t$, and $m$ monic gives $t'\circ t=1_S$; symmetrically $t\circ t'=1_{S'}$. So $t$ is an isomorphism, and it is the unique one commuting with $m,m'$.

exemplars.answer: An equivalence class of monos into $B$ under the above isomorphism; in $\mathbf{Set}$, $\mathrm{Sub}(B)\cong\mathcal{P}(B)$ as posets.
exemplars.problem: Define a subobject of $B$ and identify the subobjects of a set $B$ in $\mathbf{Set}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A subobject of $B$ is an isomorphism class of monomorphisms into $B$, where $m\sim m'$ iff $m\le m'$ and $m'\le m$; the preorder $\le$ descends to a partial order $\mathrm{Sub}(B)$ on the classes. In $\mathbf{Set}$ a mono is an injection $m\colon S\to B$, and $m\sim m'$ exactly when they have the same image, so each class is determined by the subset $m[S]\subseteq B$. The order $\le$ becomes inclusion, so $\mathrm{Sub}(B)\cong(\mathcal{P}(B),\subseteq)$.

knowledge_points.name: Subobjects as isomorphism classes of monomorphisms

anki_seeds.back: the universal $e\colon E\to A$ with $fe=ge$; in $\mathbf{Set}$, $E=\{a: f(a)=g(a)\}$.
anki_seeds.front: Equalizer of $f,g\colon A\to B$?
Every equalizer $e\colon E\to A$ is what kind of morphism?
Coequalizers are always {{c1::epimorphisms}} (dual to equalizers being monos).

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Suppose $eu=ev$ for $u,v\colon X\to E$, and set $m=eu=ev$. Then $fm=(fe)u=(ge)u=gm$, so $m$ equalizes $f,g$ and therefore factors through $e$ via a UNIQUE map $X\to E$. Both $u$ and $v$ are such factorizations ($eu=m=ev$), so uniqueness gives $u=v$. Hence $e$ is left-cancellable, i.e. a monomorphism.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Prove that every equalizer $e\colon E\to A$ of $f,g\colon A\to B$ is a monomorphism.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: From $e\circ u=e\circ v$, show the common composite equalizes $f$ and $g$, so it factors through $e$ by a unique map — and $u$, $v$ are both such factorizations. Left-cancellation comes from the uniqueness clause, not from any element chase.

knowledge_points.constraints: State the fork condition and the universal factorization; concrete descriptions in $\mathbf{Set}$ (equal-locus subset) or $\mathbf{Ab}$ (kernel of the difference).

exemplars.answer: $e\colon E\to A$ with $fe=ge$, universal; in Set $E=\{a: f(a)=g(a)\}$.
exemplars.problem: Define the equalizer of $f,g\colon A\to B$ and describe it in $\mathbf{Set}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: An equalizer of $f,g$ is $e\colon E\to A$ with $fe=ge$ that is universal: any $m\colon X\to A$ with $fm=gm$ factors as $m=eu$ for a unique $u\colon X\to E$. In $\mathbf{Set}$, $E=\{a\in A: f(a)=g(a)\}$ with $e$ the inclusion; a map $m$ landing in the equal-locus factors uniquely through $E$.

exemplars.answer: $E=\{a: f(a)=g(a)\}=\ker(f-g)$, with the inclusion $e\colon E\hookrightarrow A$.
exemplars.problem: In $\mathbf{Ab}$, identify the equalizer of homomorphisms $f,g\colon A\to B$ and relate it to a kernel.
exemplars.solution_sketch: In $\mathbf{Ab}$ the equalizer of $f,g$ is the subgroup $E=\{a\in A: f(a)=g(a)\}$ with inclusion $e$; the condition $fe=ge$ and the universal factorization are checked as in $\mathbf{Set}$, and $E$ is a subgroup because $f,g$ are homomorphisms. Since $f(a)=g(a)\iff(f-g)(a)=0$, we get $E=\ker(f-g)$. Thus equalizers in $\mathbf{Ab}$ are exactly kernels of differences, the additive analogue of the Set description.

knowledge_points.name: Equalizers, concretely in Set

knowledge_points.constraints: Abstract proofs from the universal property alone; each use of the existence or uniqueness clause must be flagged, and no elements may be used.

exemplars.problem: Prove every equalizer $e\colon E\to A$ is a monomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Suppose $eu=ev$ for $u,v\colon X\to E$, and set $m=eu=ev\colon X\to A$. Then $fm=f(eu)=(fe)u=(ge)u=g(eu)=gm$, so $m$ satisfies the equalizing condition and therefore factors through $e$ via a unique map $X\to E$. Both $u$ and $v$ are such factorizations, since $eu=m=ev$; uniqueness forces $u=v$. Hence $e$ is a monomorphism.

exemplars.answer: Epi forces $f=g$, whose equalizer is $1_A$; so $e$ is iso.
exemplars.problem: Prove that an equalizer $e\colon E\to A$ of $f,g$ that is also an epimorphism is an isomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Since $e$ equalizes, $fe=ge$; as $e$ is epi (right-cancellable) this gives $f=g$. But when $f=g$ every $m\colon X\to A$ satisfies $fm=gm$, so $1_A$ is an equalizer of $f,g$. Equalizers of a fixed pair are unique up to unique isomorphism, hence $e$ is isomorphic to $1_A$, i.e. $e$ is an isomorphism. So a regular mono (equalizer) that is epi must be iso — unlike general monos, which can be epi without being iso.

knowledge_points.name: Equalizers are monomorphisms

knowledge_points.constraints: Dualize the equalizer; concrete descriptions in $\mathbf{Set}$ (quotient by the generated equivalence relation) or $\mathbf{Ab}$ (cokernel of the difference).

exemplars.answer: $q\colon B\to Q$ with $qf=qg$, universal; in Set $Q=B/\!\sim$, $\sim$ generated by $f(a)\sim g(a)$.
exemplars.problem: Define the coequalizer of $f,g\colon A\to B$ and describe it in $\mathbf{Set}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Dually, a coequalizer is $q\colon B\to Q$ with $qf=qg$ universal among maps out of $B$ killing the difference: any $n$ with $nf=ng$ factors as $n=w q$ for a unique $w$. In $\mathbf{Set}$, $Q=B/\!\sim$ for the smallest equivalence relation with $f(a)\sim g(a)$, and $q$ is the quotient map. Dual to 'equalizers are monos', coequalizers are epis.

exemplars.problem: In $\mathbf{Ab}$, identify the coequalizer of $f,g\colon A\to B$ and relate it to a cokernel.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Dually to the equalizer-as-kernel, the coequalizer of $f,g$ in $\mathbf{Ab}$ is $q\colon B\to B/\mathrm{im}(f-g)$, the quotient by the subgroup generated by all $f(a)-g(a)$. Then $qf=qg$ since each $f(a)-g(a)\mapsto 0$, and any $n$ with $nf=ng$ kills $\mathrm{im}(f-g)$ and so factors uniquely through the quotient. As $f(a)=g(a)$ becomes $(f-g)(a)=0$ in the target, $Q=\mathrm{coker}(f-g)$; being a quotient map, $q$ is an epimorphism.

knowledge_points.name: Coequalizers by duality

anki_seeds.front: Fundamental correspondence between equivalence relations and partitions?

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: ($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $a \sim b$. For $x \in [a]$ we have $x \sim a$ and $a \sim b$, so $x \sim b$ by transitivity, giving $[a] \subseteq [b]$; using $b \sim a$ (symmetry) the same argument gives $[b] \subseteq [a]$, so $[a] = [b]$. ($\Rightarrow$) If $[a] = [b]$, then $a \in [a]$ by reflexivity, so $a \in [b]$, i.e. $a \sim b$. Deduction: if $[a] \cap [b] \ne \varnothing$, pick $x$ in both; then $x \sim a$ and $x \sim b$, so $a \sim x$ and $x \sim b$ give $a \sim b$, hence $[a] = [b]$. Contrapositively, distinct classes have empty intersection — so the classes partition $A$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on a set $A$. Prove that $[a] = [b]$ if and only if $a \sim b$, and deduce that two distinct equivalence classes are disjoint.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Use all three properties: transitivity for the inclusions, reflexivity for the converse, symmetry plus transitivity to turn a shared element into $a \sim b$.

knowledge_points.constraints: prove distinctness/uniqueness statements about the set of classes

exemplars.answer: If $[i] = [j]$ with $0 \le i, j \le 3$ then $4 \mid (i - j)$, forcing $i = j$.
exemplars.problem: Prove that the classes $[0], [1], [2], [3]$ of congruence mod $4$ are pairwise distinct, so the quotient set $\mathbb{Z}/\!\equiv_4$ has exactly $4$ elements.
exemplars.solution_sketch: If $[i] = [j]$ then $i \equiv j \pmod 4$, so $4 \mid (i - j)$. But $|i - j| \le 3$, so $i - j = 0$. Every integer is congruent to its remainder, so these four classes are all of them. $\square$

exemplars.answer: Existence: $x - \lfloor x \rfloor \in [0,1)$. Uniqueness: two such representatives differ by an integer in $(-1, 1)$, hence $0$.
exemplars.problem: On $\mathbb{R}$ with $x \sim y \iff x - y \in \mathbb{Z}$, prove every equivalence class contains exactly one element of $[0, 1)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: For $x$, the number $x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ lies in $[0,1)$ and is $\sim x$. If $r, s \in [0,1)$ are both in the class, $r - s \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $-1 < r - s < 1$, so $r = s$. $\square$

knowledge_points.name: The quotient set

knowledge_points.constraints: relate equivalence to equality (or disjointness) of classes

exemplars.answer: Both directions using reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for an equivalence relation, $a \sim b$ if and only if $[a] = [b]$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: If $a \sim b$: for $x \in [a]$, $x \sim a \sim b$ so $x \in [b]$, giving $[a] \subseteq [b]$; symmetrically $[b] \subseteq [a]$, so $[a] = [b]$. Conversely if $[a] = [b]$, then $a \in [a] = [b]$ means $a \sim b$. $\square$

exemplars.answer: A common element would force $a \sim b$.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for an equivalence relation, if $a \not\sim b$ then $[a] \cap [b] = \varnothing$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Suppose $x \in [a] \cap [b]$. Then $a \sim x$ and $b \sim x$, so $a \sim x \sim b$ gives $a \sim b$, contradicting $a \not\sim b$. Hence $[a] \cap [b] = \varnothing$. $\square$

knowledge_points.constraints: show covering plus pairwise disjointness; and the converse direction

exemplars.answer: If two classes meet, they are equal.
exemplars.problem: Prove: distinct equivalence classes are disjoint, so the classes partition the set.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Each $a$ lies in $[a]$ (reflexivity), so classes cover the set. If $x \in [a] \cap [b]$, then $a \sim x \sim b$, so $a \sim b$ and $[a] = [b]$. Hence two classes are equal or disjoint: a partition. $\square$

exemplars.answer: Define $a \sim b$ iff same block; check the three properties.
exemplars.problem: Prove: a partition $\mathcal{Q}$ of $A$ induces an equivalence relation whose classes are the blocks of $\mathcal{Q}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Define $a \sim b$ iff $a, b$ lie in the same block. Every $a$ is in some block (reflexive); same-block is symmetric; if $a, b$ share a block and $b, c$ share a block, that block is common (blocks are disjoint), so $a, c$ share it (transitive). The class of $a$ is its block. $\square$

anki_seeds.front: Equivalence of categories: definition?
A functor is an equivalence iff it is {{c1::fully faithful}} and {{c2::essentially surjective}}.

anki_seeds.back: every object of the target is isomorphic to some $FC$ in the image of $F$.
anki_seeds.front: A functor $F$ is essentially surjective when...

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Essential surjectivity: for any object $D$ of $\mathcal D$, the component $\varepsilon_D\colon FGD\xrightarrow{\cong}D$ shows $D\cong F(GD)$. Faithfulness: naturality of $\eta$ at $f\colon A\to B$ gives $GF(f)\circ\eta_A=\eta_B\circ f$, so $f=\eta_B^{-1}\circ GF(f)\circ\eta_A$ — $f$ is recovered from $GF(f)$. If $Ff=Fg$ then $GFf=GFg$, hence $f=g$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Let $(F,G,\eta,\varepsilon)$ be an equivalence of categories, with natural isomorphisms $\eta\colon 1_{\mathcal C}\xRightarrow{\cong}GF$ and $\varepsilon\colon FG\xRightarrow{\cong}1_{\mathcal D}$. Prove that $F$ is faithful and essentially surjective.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Essential surjectivity is read straight off the components of $\varepsilon$. For faithfulness, use naturality of $\eta$ to solve for $f$ in terms of $GF(f)$, namely $f=\eta_B^{-1}\circ GF(f)\circ\eta_A$, so $Ff=Fg$ forces $f=g$.

knowledge_points.constraints: State all four pieces $(F,G,\eta,\varepsilon)$ with the direction of each natural iso; symmetry/closure proofs may only invert or compose natural isomorphisms.

exemplars.answer: Functors $F,G$ with $GF\cong 1_{\mathcal C}$ and $FG\cong 1_{\mathcal D}$ (natural isos), not equalities.
exemplars.problem: Define an equivalence of categories $\mathcal C\simeq\mathcal D$ and contrast it with an isomorphism of categories.
exemplars.solution_sketch: An equivalence is a pair $F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$, $G\colon\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ with natural isomorphisms $\eta\colon 1_{\mathcal C}\xRightarrow{\cong}GF$ and $\varepsilon\colon FG\xRightarrow{\cong}1_{\mathcal D}$. An isomorphism of categories would demand $GF=1_{\mathcal C}$ and $FG=1_{\mathcal D}$ on the nose; equivalence relaxes this to hold only up to natural isomorphism, which is the appropriate notion of sameness for categories.

exemplars.answer: The quasi-inverse together with the inverse natural isos witnesses the reverse equivalence.
exemplars.problem: Prove that equivalence of categories is symmetric: if $\mathcal C\simeq\mathcal D$ then $\mathcal D\simeq\mathcal C$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: An equivalence gives $F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$, $G\colon\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ and natural isomorphisms $\eta\colon 1_{\mathcal C}\xRightarrow{\cong}GF$, $\varepsilon\colon FG\xRightarrow{\cong}1_{\mathcal D}$. To exhibit $\mathcal D\simeq\mathcal C$ use the pair $(G,F)$: since inverses of natural isomorphisms are natural isomorphisms, $\varepsilon^{-1}\colon 1_{\mathcal D}\xRightarrow{\cong}FG$ and $\eta^{-1}\colon GF\xRightarrow{\cong}1_{\mathcal C}$ are the required natural isos. Hence $(G,F,\varepsilon^{-1},\eta^{-1})$ is an equivalence and $\mathcal D\simeq\mathcal C$.

knowledge_points.name: Definition via natural isomorphisms

knowledge_points.constraints: Only the easy direction is proved in full ($\varepsilon_D$ gives essential surjectivity; $f=\eta_B^{-1}\circ GFf\circ\eta_A$ gives faithfulness); the converse is stated with its choice-based construction sketched.

exemplars.answer: $F$ is an equivalence iff it is fully faithful and essentially surjective (every $D\cong FC$ for some $C$).
exemplars.problem: State the characterization of when a functor $F$ is part of an equivalence, and define its essential-surjectivity clause.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $F$ is essentially surjective if every object $D$ of $\mathcal D$ is isomorphic to $FC$ for some object $C$. Theorem: $F$ extends to an equivalence iff $F$ is fully faithful and essentially surjective. Given these, choose for each $D$ an object $GD$ with iso $FGD\cong D$; full faithfulness transports morphisms uniquely to make $G$ a functor and the chosen isos natural.

exemplars.answer: $\varepsilon_D\colon FGD\cong D$ gives ess. surjectivity; naturality of $\eta$ recovers $f$ from $GFf$.
exemplars.problem: Prove the easy direction: if $(F,G,\eta,\varepsilon)$ is an equivalence then $F$ is faithful and essentially surjective.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Essential surjectivity: for any object $D$, the component $\varepsilon_D\colon FGD\xrightarrow{\cong}D$ shows $D\cong F(GD)$. Faithfulness: naturality of $\eta\colon 1_{\mathcal C}\xRightarrow{\cong}GF$ gives $GF(f)\circ\eta_A=\eta_B\circ f$, so $f=\eta_B^{-1}\circ GF(f)\circ\eta_A$; hence $f$ is recovered from $GF(f)$. If $Ff=Fg$ then applying $G$ gives $GFf=GFg$, so $f=g$. Thus $F$ is faithful and essentially surjective.

knowledge_points.name: The fully faithful + essentially surjective test

knowledge_points.constraints: Instances limited to $\mathbf{FinVect}_k\simeq\mathbf{Mat}_k$ and the two-object indiscrete groupoid $\simeq\mathbf 1$; the non-isomorphism claim is always settled by counting objects.

exemplars.answer: $F(n)=k^n$ is fully faithful and essentially surjective.
exemplars.problem: Show $\mathbf{FinVect}_k\simeq\mathbf{Mat}_k$, where $\mathbf{Mat}_k$ has objects $n\in\mathbb N$ and morphisms $m\to n$ the $n\times m$ matrices.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Define $F\colon\mathbf{Mat}_k\to\mathbf{FinVect}_k$, $F(n)=k^n$, $F(M)=$ the linear map with matrix $M$. Linear maps $k^m\to k^n$ correspond bijectively to $n\times m$ matrices, so $F$ is fully faithful; every finite-dimensional space has a basis, hence is isomorphic to some $k^n$, so $F$ is essentially surjective. By the characterization $F$ is an equivalence. It is not an isomorphism of categories (the two have different numbers of objects), showing equivalence is strictly weaker.

exemplars.answer: The unique functor $\mathbf I\to\mathbf 1$ is an equivalence; the object counts differ, so it is not an isomorphism.
exemplars.problem: Let $\mathbf I$ be the groupoid with two objects $0,1$ and exactly one morphism between each ordered pair of objects. Show $\mathbf I\simeq\mathbf 1$ (the terminal category) but $\mathbf I\not\cong\mathbf 1$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $F\colon\mathbf I\to\mathbf 1$ be the only functor and $G\colon\mathbf 1\to\mathbf I$ pick the object $0$; then $FG=1_{\mathbf 1}$ on the nose. For $GF$ (which sends everything to $0$) define $\eta_X\colon X\to 0$ to be the unique morphism: each is an isomorphism, and naturality is automatic since $\mathbf I$ has exactly one morphism between any two objects. So $\eta\colon 1_{\mathbf I}\xRightarrow{\cong}GF$ and $\mathbf I\simeq\mathbf 1$. They are not isomorphic as categories, since $\mathbf I$ has two objects and $\mathbf 1$ has one.

knowledge_points.name: An equivalence that is not an isomorphism

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: First, $\langle 3, x \rangle = \{p \in \mathbb{Z}[x] : 3 \mid p(0)\}$, a proper ideal since $1 \notin$ it. Suppose $\langle 3, x\rangle = \langle f \rangle$. Then $f \mid 3$, so $f$ is a constant $\pm 1$ or $\pm 3$. If $f = \pm 1$ the ideal would be all of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, contradicting properness; if $f = \pm 3$ then $f \nmid x$ (that would need $3$ to divide the coefficient $1$), contradicting $x \in \langle f \rangle$. So no single generator exists. In $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ this cannot happen: division with remainder by degree makes $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ a Euclidean domain, and in a Euclidean domain a nonzero element of least norm in an ideal generates it — every Euclidean domain is a PID.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Show that the ideal $\langle 3, x \rangle$ of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is not principal, and explain why no ideal of $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ can fail in this way.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Describe the ideal concretely, then rule out both candidate generators. The contrast: $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ has a degree norm with division, so a least-degree element of any ideal generates it.

exemplars.problem: A Euclidean domain carries a norm allowing division with smaller remainder. In the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ with $N(a + bi) = a^2 + b^2$, compute $N(3 + 2i)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $N(3 + 2i) = 3^2 + 2^2 = 13$. ($N$ is multiplicative: $N(zw) = N(z)N(w)$.)

exemplars.problem: Divide $7 + 2i$ by $2 - i$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$: find $q, r$ with $7 + 2i = (2 - i)q + r$ and $N(r) < N(2 - i)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Exact quotient: $\frac{7+2i}{2-i} = \frac{(7+2i)(2+i)}{5} = \frac{12 + 11i}{5} = 2.4 + 2.2i$; round to the nearest Gaussian integer $q = 2 + 2i$. Then $r = 7 + 2i - (2-i)(2+2i) = 7 + 2i - (6 + 2i) = 1$, and $N(1) = 1 < 5 = N(2 - i)$.

exemplars.answer: In a nonzero ideal $I$, pick $d \neq 0$ of minimal norm. For any $a \in I$, write $a = qd + r$ with $r = 0$ or $N(r) < N(d)$; since $r = a - qd \in I$, minimality forces $r = 0$. So $I = \langle d \rangle$.

anki_seeds.front: Standard precedence of $\neg$, $\land$, $\lor$?

diagnostic_exemplar.answer:
By the standard precedence ($
eg$, then $\land$, then $\lor$) the first formula is $(P \land 
eg Q) \lor R = (\mathrm{F} \land \mathrm{F}) \lor \mathrm{T} = \mathrm{T}$. The second is $P \land (
eg Q \lor R) = \mathrm{F} \land (\mathrm{F} \lor \mathrm{T}) = \mathrm{F} \land \mathrm{T} = \mathrm{F}$. The values differ, so the parentheses do change the meaning.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Evaluate $P \land \neg Q \lor R$ and $P \land (\neg Q \lor R)$ at $P$ = F, $Q$ = T, $R$ = T, and state whether the parentheses change the value.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Group the unparenthesised formula by precedence before evaluating, then compare with the parenthesised version at the same assignment.

knowledge_points.constraints: precedence order $\neg$, $\land$, $\lor$; identify the main connective

exemplars.problem: Insert parentheses to show how $\neg P \lor Q \land R$ is grouped by the standard precedence ($\neg$, then $\land$, then $\lor$).
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\neg$ binds tightest and applies only to $P$; $\land$ binds tighter than $\lor$, so $Q \land R$ groups before the disjunction.

exemplars.problem: In $\neg P \lor Q \land R$, which connective is applied last?
exemplars.solution_sketch: After grouping, the formula is a disjunction of $\neg P$ and $Q \land R$, so $\lor$ is the main connective.

knowledge_points.name: Operator precedence

knowledge_points.constraints: connectives limited to $\neg, \land, \lor$; up to 3 variables; single assignment of truth values

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\neg P \lor Q \land R$ at $P$ = T, $Q$ = F, $R$ = T.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Group as $(\neg P) \lor (Q \land R)$. $\neg P$ = F and $Q \land R$ = F $\land$ T = F, so F $\lor$ F = F.

exemplars.problem: Evaluate $\neg P \land Q$ at $P$ = F, $Q$ = T.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\neg P$ = T, so $\neg P \land Q$ = T $\land$ T = T.

exemplars.problem: At $P$ = F, $Q$ = T, evaluate both $\neg(P \lor Q)$ and $\neg P \lor Q$. Do they agree?
exemplars.solution_sketch: $P \lor Q$ = T so its negation is F; but $\neg P$ = T already makes $\neg P \lor Q$ true. Parentheses determine what the negation applies to.

exemplars.problem: At $P$ = T, $Q$ = F, $R$ = F, evaluate $P \land (\neg Q \lor R)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\neg Q$ = T, so $\neg Q \lor R$ = T; then T $\land$ T = T.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Given $(a,b)\colon f\to f'$ and $(a',b')\colon f'\to f''$, compute $f''\circ(a'\circ a)=(f''\circ a')\circ a=(b'\circ f')\circ a=b'\circ(f'\circ a)=b'\circ(b\circ f)=(b'\circ b)\circ f$, using associativity and the two given squares. So $(a'\circ a,\,b'\circ b)$ makes the outer square commute and is a morphism $f\to f''$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: In the arrow category $\mathcal{C}^{\to}$, a morphism from $f\colon A\to B$ to $f'\colon A'\to B'$ is a pair $(a\colon A\to A',\,b\colon B\to B')$ with $f'\circ a=b\circ f$. Prove that the componentwise composite of two such morphisms is again a morphism of $\mathcal{C}^{\to}$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Paste the two commuting squares: start from $f''\circ(a'\circ a)$ and push $f''$ across the second square, then across the first, until it emerges as $(b'\circ b)\circ f$. Only associativity and the two given squares are used.

knowledge_points.constraints: Categories of structured sets only ($\mathbf{Mon}$, $\mathbf{Grp}$, $\mathbf{Poset}$, $\mathbf{Top}$); verification means checking identity maps qualify and composites preserve the structure; no size/foundational issues raised.

exemplars.answer: Objects are monoids, morphisms are monoid homomorphisms; identity maps and composites of homomorphisms are homomorphisms.
exemplars.problem: Describe the objects and morphisms of $\mathbf{Mon}$ (monoids) and check identities and composites are legal.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Objects are monoids $(M,\cdot,e)$; a morphism $M\to N$ is a function $f$ with $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$ and $f(e_M)=e_N$. The identity function is a homomorphism, and if $f,g$ are homomorphisms so is $g\circ f$: $g(f(xy))=g(f(x)f(y))=g(f(x))g(f(y))$ and $g(f(e))=e$. Associativity and units are inherited from $\mathbf{Set}$, so $\mathbf{Mon}$ is a category.

exemplars.answer: $\mathbf{Grp}$: groups and group homomorphisms; $\mathbf{Poset}$: posets and monotone (order-preserving) maps.
exemplars.problem: State what the objects and morphisms are in $\mathbf{Grp}$ and in $\mathbf{Poset}$.

exemplars.problem: A group $G$ gives a one-object category $BG$. What special property do all its morphisms have?
exemplars.solution_sketch: $BG$ has one object $*$ with $\mathrm{Hom}(*,*)=G$ and composition the group product. Each $g\in G$ has a two-sided inverse $g^{-1}$, so $g$ is an isomorphism in $BG$. Thus $BG$ is a category in which every arrow is invertible, i.e. a groupoid with one object.

exemplars.answer: It is the poset $0\le 1$ viewed as a category; composition is forced and associative.

exemplars.answer: Objects are morphisms $f\colon A\to B$ of $\mathcal{C}$; a morphism $f\to f'$ is a commuting square.
exemplars.problem: Describe the arrow category $\mathcal{C}^{\to}$: what is an object and what is a morphism?
exemplars.solution_sketch: An object is an arrow $f\colon A\to B$ in $\mathcal{C}$. A morphism from $f\colon A\to B$ to $f'\colon A'\to B'$ is a pair $(a\colon A\to A',\, b\colon B\to B')$ with $f'\circ a = b\circ f$ (the square commutes). Componentwise identities and composition inherit the category axioms from $\mathcal{C}$, and pasting commuting squares gives a commuting square, so $\mathcal{C}^{\to}$ is a category.

exemplars.answer: Objects are pairs $(C,D)$; morphisms are pairs $(f,g)$; composition and identities are componentwise.
exemplars.problem: Given categories $\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}$, describe the product category $\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{D}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\mathrm{Hom}((C,D),(C',D'))=\mathrm{Hom}(C,C')\times\mathrm{Hom}(D,D')$ with $(f',g')\circ(f,g)=(f'\circ f, g'\circ g)$ and $1_{(C,D)}=(1_C,1_D)$; the axioms hold in each coordinate.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Every integer leaves one of the four remainders $0, 1, 2, 3$ on division by $4$. Given five integers, two of them must leave the same remainder, since there are only four remainders available. If $a = 4s + r$ and $b = 4t + r$ share the remainder $r$, then $a - b = 4(s - t)$, so $4 \mid (a - b)$. This proves existence without exhibiting the pair — a nonconstructive existence proof.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Prove: among any five integers, there are two whose difference is divisible by $4$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Classify the integers by remainder mod $4$; with five integers and four classes two must share a class, and equal remainders make the difference a multiple of $4$.

exemplars.solution_sketch: For $2 \le k \le n + 1$, $k$ is one of the factors of $(n+1)!$, so $k \mid (n+1)!$ and hence $k \mid (n+1)! + k$; since $(n+1)! + k > k$, that number is composite. That is $n$ consecutive composites. $\square$

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: A component's lifetime is exponential with rate $\lambda = 0.25$ per hour, and it has already survived $6$ hours. Using $e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$, find the probability it survives at least $4$ more hours, to four decimal places.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Memorylessness discards the $6$ hours: $P = e^{-0.25 \cdot 4} = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$.

knowledge_points.constraints: lambda t comes out to a value whose e^{-lambda t} is supplied in the problem; answers to 4 decimal places

exemplars.problem: $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda = 0.25$ per minute. Find $E[X]$ in minutes.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The mean of an exponential variable is $\frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{0.25} = 4$ minutes.

exemplars.problem: An exponential variable has mean $10$. Find its rate $\lambda$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\lambda = \frac{1}{\text{mean}} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1$.

exemplars.problem: $X$ is exponential with rate $\lambda = 0.5$. Using $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$, find the median of $X$ to four decimal places.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Solve $e^{-\lambda m} = \frac{1}{2}$: $m = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \frac{0.6931}{0.5} = 1.3862$.

exemplars.solution_sketch: By memorylessness the past $5$ hours are irrelevant: $P(X > 3) = e^{-0.5 \cdot 3} = e^{-1.5} \approx 0.2231$.

exemplars.problem: Buses arrive as a Poisson process at rate $3$ per hour, so the waiting time between buses is exponential. Find its mean, in minutes.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Mean waiting time $= \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{3}$ hour $= 20$ minutes.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Currying sends $g\colon X\times A\to B$ to the unique $\hat g\colon X\to B^A$ with $\mathrm{ev}\circ(\hat g\times 1_A)=g$; uncurrying sends $h\colon X\to B^A$ to $\mathrm{ev}\circ(h\times 1_A)$. Uncurrying after currying returns $g$ by the defining equation. Currying after uncurrying returns $h$: $h$ satisfies the defining equation of the curry of $\mathrm{ev}\circ(h\times 1_A)$, and the universal property says there is exactly one such map. So the two operations are mutually inverse, giving the bijection.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: From the universal property of the exponential $B^A$ (evaluation $\mathrm{ev}\colon B^A\times A\to B$ with unique currying), deduce the bijection $\mathrm{Hom}(X\times A,B)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(X,B^A)$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Define currying and uncurrying from the universal property and check the two round trips. One direction is just the defining equation of $\mathrm{ev}$; the other needs the uniqueness clause, which says no other map satisfies that equation.
