exemplars.problem: Define the exponential object $B^A$ by its universal property and identify it in $\mathbf{Set}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: An exponential $B^A$ carries $\mathrm{ev}\colon B^A\times A\to B$ such that for every $g\colon X\times A\to B$ there is a unique $\hat g\colon X\to B^A$ (its curry) with $\mathrm{ev}\circ(\hat g\times 1_A)=g$. In $\mathbf{Set}$, $B^A=\{$functions $A\to B\}$, $\mathrm{ev}(f,a)=f(a)$, and $\hat g(x)=(a\mapsto g(x,a))$ is the unique such map.

exemplars.answer: The relative pseudocomplement $a\Rightarrow b=\bigvee\{x : x\wedge a\le b\}$, when it exists (Heyting implication).
exemplars.problem: In a poset (as a category) with finite meets, identify the exponential object $b^a$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: In a poset, the product $x\times a$ is the meet $x\wedge a$, so the currying bijection $\mathrm{Hom}(X\times A,B)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(X,B^A)$ becomes the equivalence $x\wedge a\le b\iff x\le b^a$ (hom-sets have at most one element). Thus $b^a$ is the largest element whose meet with $a$ lies below $b$, i.e. the relative pseudocomplement $a\Rightarrow b=\bigvee\{x:x\wedge a\le b\}$, and evaluation is the counit $(a\Rightarrow b)\wedge a\le b$. A poset with finite meets, a top and all such exponentials is cartesian closed; it is a Heyting algebra only if it is moreover a bounded lattice, since a Heyting algebra is by definition a bounded lattice with implication. Cartesian closure supplies neither joins nor a bottom: $(\mathbb Z\cup\{+\infty\},\le)$ has all meets, the top $+\infty$, and exponentials ($b^a=+\infty$ when $a\le b$ and $b^a=b$ otherwise), yet it has no least element.

knowledge_points.name: Exponentials via currying in Set

knowledge_points.constraints: Derive the bijection and its naturality from the universal property alone; every identification of two maps must go through the uniqueness of currying.

exemplars.answer: Currying $g\mapsto\hat g$ and uncurrying are mutually inverse, natural in $X$.
exemplars.problem: Deduce the natural bijection $\mathrm{Hom}(X\times A,B)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(X,B^A)$ from the universal property of $B^A$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The universal property gives, for each $g\colon X\times A\to B$, a unique curry $\hat g\colon X\to B^A$; conversely each $h\colon X\to B^A$ uncurries to $\mathrm{ev}\circ(h\times 1_A)$, and these operations are mutually inverse. Hence $\mathrm{Hom}(X\times A,B)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(X,B^A)$; naturality in $X$ holds because precomposing $g$ by $k\times 1_A$ corresponds to precomposing $\hat g$ by $k$. This is precisely the adjunction $(-\times A)\dashv(-)^A$.

exemplars.answer: $k^A\circ\hat g$ satisfies the defining equation of the curry of $k\circ g$, so uniqueness identifies the two.
exemplars.problem: Prove that currying is also natural in the target: for $k\colon B\to B'$ and $g\colon X\times A\to B$, show $\widehat{k\circ g}=k^A\circ\hat g$, where $k^A\colon B^A\to B'^A$ is the unique map with $\mathrm{ev}\circ(k^A\times 1_A)=k\circ\mathrm{ev}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: First, $k^A$ is well defined: it is the curry of $k\circ\mathrm{ev}\colon B^A\times A\to B'$, so $\mathrm{ev}\circ(k^A\times 1_A)=k\circ\mathrm{ev}$. Now uncurry $k^A\circ\hat g$, using $(u\circ v)\times 1_A=(u\times 1_A)\circ(v\times 1_A)$: $\mathrm{ev}\circ((k^A\circ\hat g)\times 1_A)=\mathrm{ev}\circ(k^A\times 1_A)\circ(\hat g\times 1_A)=k\circ\mathrm{ev}\circ(\hat g\times 1_A)=k\circ g$. So $k^A\circ\hat g$ is a curry of $k\circ g$, and the universal property says there is exactly one, whence $\widehat{k\circ g}=k^A\circ\hat g$. Together with naturality in $X$ this makes $\mathrm{Hom}(X\times A,B)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(X,B^A)$ natural in both variables, and it is what makes $(-)^A$ a functor.

anki_seeds.front: Every integral domain embeds in a ______.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: It is $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}) = \{p + q\sqrt{2} : p, q \in \mathbb{Q}\}$. Every quotient of elements of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$ lies there: for $c + d\sqrt2 \ne 0$, $\frac{a+b\sqrt2}{c+d\sqrt2} = \frac{(a+b\sqrt2)(c-d\sqrt2)}{c^2 - 2d^2}$, and $c^2 - 2d^2 \ne 0$ because $\sqrt2$ is irrational; the result has the form $p + q\sqrt2$ with $p, q \in \mathbb{Q}$. Conversely $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ is a field containing $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$, and any field containing a domain $D$ contains a copy of $\mathrm{Frac}(D)$ via $a/b \mapsto ab^{-1}$; since each $p + q\sqrt2$ is such a quotient, $\mathrm{Frac}(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]) = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Identify the field of fractions of the integral domain $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{2}] = \{a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ as an explicit subfield of $\mathbb{R}$, and justify your answer.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Rationalise the denominator with the conjugate; the norm $c^2 - 2d^2$ is nonzero by irrationality of $\sqrt2$. Then use that $\mathrm{Frac}(D)$ embeds in every field containing $D$, so it is the smallest such field.

knowledge_points.constraints: the transitivity and denominator-closure arguments, each localizing exactly where the domain hypothesis is used; well-definedness of + or x checked on one representative change

exemplars.answer: Suppose $(a,b) \sim (c,d)$ and $(c,d) \sim (e,f)$: $ad = bc$ and $cf = de$. Then $adf = bcf = bde$, so $d(af - be) = 0$. Since $d \neq 0$ and $D$ has no zero divisors, $af = be$, i.e. $(a,b) \sim (e,f)$. The cancellation of $d$ is exactly where the domain property is used.
exemplars.problem: Let $D$ be an integral domain. On $D \times (D \setminus \{0\})$ define $(a, b) \sim (c, d) \iff ad = bc$. Prove that $\sim$ is transitive, and point out where you use that $D$ is a domain.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Multiply the two defining equations to a common expression and cancel $d$ — legal only without zero divisors.

exemplars.answer: Denominators must be nonzero: $b, d \neq 0$ gives $bd \neq 0$ precisely because a domain has no zero divisors. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$, $b = 2$ and $d = 3$ are nonzero yet $bd = 0$, so the sum would have a zero denominator — the construction breaks.
exemplars.problem: Fractions are added by $\frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ad + bc}{bd}$. Why does the denominator $bd$ stay legal, and where does that fail in a ring with zero divisors?
exemplars.solution_sketch: Closure of $D \setminus \{0\}$ under multiplication is equivalent to having no zero divisors.

exemplars.answer: $\iota(a + b) = \frac{a+b}{1} = \frac{a}{1} + \frac{b}{1}$ and $\iota(ab) = \frac{ab}{1} = \frac{a}{1} \cdot \frac{b}{1}$ by the fraction operations with denominator $1$. Injective: $\frac{a}{1} = \frac{b}{1}$ means $a \cdot 1 = 1 \cdot b$, i.e. $a = b$.
exemplars.problem: Prove that $\iota : D \to \mathrm{Frac}(D)$, $\iota(a) = \frac{a}{1}$, is an injective ring homomorphism.

exemplars.answer: Map $\frac{a}{b} \mapsto ab^{-1} \in K$ (defined since $b \neq 0$ is invertible in $K$); it is well defined ($ad = bc \implies ab^{-1} = cd^{-1}$), a ring homomorphism, and injective since a nonzero fraction maps to a nonzero element — its image is a subfield isomorphic to $\mathrm{Frac}(D)$. Hence $\mathbb{Q}$ is (up to isomorphism) the smallest field containing $\mathbb{Z}$.
exemplars.problem: Show that any field $K$ containing an integral domain $D$ (as a subring) contains a subfield isomorphic to $\mathrm{Frac}(D)$. What does this say about $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$?
exemplars.solution_sketch: The universal property, lite: fractions have nowhere to go but $ab^{-1}$, so $\mathrm{Frac}(D)$ embeds in every field around $D$.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: $(a+b)^5 = a^5 + b^5$: by the binomial theorem the middle coefficients are $\binom{5}{1} = 5$, $\binom{5}{2} = 10$, $\binom{5}{3} = 10$, $\binom{5}{4} = 5$, each divisible by $5$, so those terms are $0$ in characteristic $5$. A field with $25 = 5^2$ elements has characteristic $5$: its prime subfield is $\mathbb{Z}_5$, and a finite field of order $p^{n}$ has characteristic the prime $p$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: In a commutative ring of characteristic $5$, expand $(a + b)^5$ in simplest form and justify which terms vanish. Then give the characteristic of a field with $25$ elements.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Only the two end terms of the binomial expansion survive — this is the Frobenius map $x \mapsto x^{p}$. A finite field has prime-power order and characteristic that prime.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: By the classification, $G$ is the product of its $2$-primary and $3$-primary parts, of orders $4$ and $9$. The order-$4$ part is $\mathbb{Z}_4$ or $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$; the latter has three elements of order $2$, so it must be $\mathbb{Z}_4$. The order-$9$ part is $\mathbb{Z}_9$ or $\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_3$; the latter has eight elements of order $3$, so it must be $\mathbb{Z}_9$. Hence $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_9 \cong \mathbb{Z}_{36}$, and the invariant-factor form is the single factor $\mathbb{Z}_{36}$ (since $\gcd(4,9) = 1$).
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: An abelian group $G$ of order $36$ has exactly one element of order $2$ and exactly two elements of order $3$. Identify $G$ up to isomorphism and give its invariant-factor form.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Split into $p$-primary parts, then use the counts of elements of order $p$ to pick the right partition; coprime orders merge into one invariant factor.

knowledge_points.constraints: orders <= 16; distinguish candidate decompositions by counts of elements of a given order

exemplars.problem: Which abelian group of order $8$ has exactly $3$ elements of order $2$?
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\mathbb{Z}_8$ has one element of order $2$; $\mathbb{Z}_2^3$ has seven; $\mathbb{Z}_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ has $(2,0), (0,1), (2,1)$ — exactly three.

exemplars.problem: An abelian group of order $16$ has every non-identity element of order $2$. Identify it up to isomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Any factor $\mathbb{Z}_{2^k}$ with $k \ge 2$ would contribute an element of order $4$; so all factors are $\mathbb{Z}_2$.

knowledge_points.name: Identifying an abelian group by its element orders

topics.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Finite Abelian Groups

anki_seeds.back: there is a bijection $\{1, 2, \dots, n\} \to A$.
anki_seeds.front: "$A$ has $n$ elements" formally means...
For finite sets, an injection $A \to B$ exists iff...

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: The map $k \mapsto k + 9$ sends $\{1, \dots, 90\}$ into $A$; it is injective (adding $9$ is) and onto ($a \in A$ equals $(a-9) + 9$ with $1 \le a - 9 \le 90$), so it is a bijection and $|A| = 90$. Likewise $k \mapsto k + 199$ is a bijection $\{1, \dots, 10\} \to B$, so $|B| = 10$. The sets are disjoint, since every element of $A$ is at most $99$ and every element of $B$ is at least $200$. Concatenating the two counting bijections gives $h : \{1, \dots, 100\} \to A \cup B$ with $h(j) = j + 9$ for $1 \le j \le 90$ and $h(j) = j + 109$ for $91 \le j \le 100$ (so $h(91) = 200$ and $h(100) = 209$); $h$ is a bijection, hence $|A \cup B| = 100 = |A| + |B|$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Let $A = \{10, 11, \dots, 99\}$ and $B = \{200, 201, \dots, 209\}$. Prove that $|A| = 90$ and that $|A \cup B| = 100$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Exhibit a shift bijection from an initial segment for each set, then glue the two bijections — legitimate because the sets are disjoint.

knowledge_points.constraints: exhibit an explicit bijection from $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and verify both properties

exemplars.problem: Prove that $\{2, 4, 6, \dots, 2n\}$ has exactly $n$ elements by exhibiting a bijection with $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The map $k \mapsto 2k$ is injective ($2a = 2b \Rightarrow a = b$) and surjective (every listed even number is $2k$ for some $1 \le k \le n$). $\square$

exemplars.problem: Prove that $\{5, 6, 7, \dots, 17\}$ has $13$ elements.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The shift $k \mapsto k + 4$ is injective, and its outputs for $k = 1, \dots, 13$ are exactly $5, \dots, 17$. $\square$

knowledge_points.name: Size as a bijection with {1, ..., n}

knowledge_points.constraints: connect bijections/injections to size comparisons via pigeonhole

exemplars.answer: Compose bijections with the counting bijections; $3 > 2$ kills injectivity.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for finite sets, if there is a bijection $A \to B$ then $|A| = |B|$; and there is no bijection $\{1,2,3\} \to \{a, b\}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Composing $\{1, \dots, m\} \to A \to B \to \{1, \dots, n\}$ gives a bijection between counting sets, forcing $m = n$. And any map $\{1,2,3\} \to \{a,b\}$ repeats a value by pigeonhole, so no bijection exists. $\square$

exemplars.answer: Pigeonhole rules out $|A| > |B|$; listing elements builds the injection otherwise.
exemplars.problem: Prove: for finite sets, an injection $A \to B$ exists if and only if $|A| \le |B|$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: If $f : A \to B$ is injective then $|A| = |f(A)| \le |B|$. Conversely if $|A| \le |B|$, send the $i$-th element of $A$ to the $i$-th element of $B$ — injective since the elements are distinct. $\square$

knowledge_points.name: Bijections and matching sizes

knowledge_points.constraints: build the new bijection explicitly from the given ones

exemplars.problem: Prove: if $A$ and $B$ are finite and disjoint, then $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B|$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Given bijections $\{1, \dots, m\} \to A$ and $\{1, \dots, n\} \to B$, map $i \le m$ into $A$ and $m + j$ (for $1 \le j \le n$) into $B$. Disjointness makes this well-defined and bijective onto $A \cup B$. $\square$

exemplars.answer: Extend a counting bijection by sending $n + 1 \mapsto a$.
exemplars.problem: Prove: if $A$ is finite and $a \notin A$, then $|A \cup \{a\}| = |A| + 1$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Take a bijection $f : \{1, \dots, n\} \to A$ and define $g = f$ on $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with $g(n+1) = a$. Since $a \notin A$, $g$ is injective, and it is onto $A \cup \{a\}$. $\square$

knowledge_points.name: Cardinality arithmetic

anki_seeds.front: $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field iff...

anki_seeds.back: Exactly the prime powers $p^n$ (one field of each order, up to isomorphism).
anki_seeds.front: Possible orders of finite fields?
Fermat inverse formula in $\mathbb{Z}_p$?

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Take $F = \mathbb{Z}_3[x]/\langle x^2 + 1\rangle$. The polynomial $x^2 + 1$ has no root in $\mathbb{Z}_3$ ($0, 1, 2$ give $1, 2, 2$), so being of degree $2$ it is irreducible; hence $\langle x^2+1\rangle$ is maximal and the quotient is a field. Its elements are $a + b\alpha$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}_3$ and $\alpha$ the class of $x$, so $|F| = 3^2 = 9$. Since $\alpha^2 = -1 = 2$, we get $\alpha \cdot 2\alpha = 2\alpha^2 = 2 \cdot 2 = 4 = 1$, so $\alpha^{-1} = 2\alpha$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Describe a field with exactly $9$ elements, justifying that it is a field, and compute the inverse of $\alpha$, the root of the polynomial you adjoin.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Adjoin a root of an irreducible quadratic over $\mathbb{Z}_3$ (Kronecker) to get $3^2$ elements, then invert $\alpha$ using $\alpha^2 = 2$.

knowledge_points.constraints: p <= 13; linear and quadratic equations solved by field arithmetic

exemplars.problem: Solve $3x + 5 = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_7$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $3x = -4 = 3$, and multiplying by $3^{-1} = 5$ gives $x = 15 = 1$. Check: $3 + 5 = 8 \equiv 1$.

exemplars.problem: Find all solutions of $x^2 = 2$ in $\mathbb{Z}_7$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $3^2 = 9 \equiv 2$ and $4^2 = 16 \equiv 2$; a quadratic over a field has at most two roots.

knowledge_points.name: Arithmetic in Z_p: inverses and linear equations

knowledge_points.constraints: the Bezout proof; Fermat-inverse computations with p <= 11

exemplars.answer: For $a \neq 0$, $\gcd(a, p) = 1$, so Bezout gives $ax + py = 1$, i.e. $ax \equiv 1$: every nonzero element is invertible.
exemplars.problem: Prove that $\mathbb{Z}_p$ ($p$ prime) is a field.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Primality makes every nonzero residue coprime to $p$; extended Euclid produces the inverse.

exemplars.problem: Use Fermat's little theorem to express $a^{-1}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_p$, and compute $4^{-1}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_7$ this way.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $a \cdot a^{p-2} = a^{p-1} = 1$. And indeed $4 \cdot 2 = 8 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$.

knowledge_points.name: Why Z_p is a field; Fermat inverses

knowledge_points.constraints: existence/size questions for orders <= 27; construction via irreducible polynomials may be quoted

exemplars.answer: No: every finite field has prime-power order, and $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ is not a prime power.
exemplars.problem: Is there a field with exactly $6$ elements?
exemplars.solution_sketch: A finite field is a vector space over its prime subfield $\mathbb{Z}_p$, so its size is $p^n$.

exemplars.problem: Describe a field with $4$ elements.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Quotient by an irreducible quadratic over $\mathbb{Z}_2$; the four remainders form a field.

knowledge_points.name: Finite fields beyond Z_p: order p^n

anki_seeds.front: First isomorphism theorem?

anki_seeds.back: Find a surjective homomorphism out of $G$ whose kernel is exactly $N$; the image is the quotient.
anki_seeds.front: Strategy to identify a quotient $G/N$?

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Let $\varphi : \mathbb{Z}_{12} \to \mathbb{Z}_{12}$, $\varphi(x) = 3x$. Apply the first isomorphism theorem: what is $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/\{0,4,8\}$ isomorphic to?
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: $\ker\varphi = \{0,4,8\}$ and $\mathrm{im}\,\varphi = \langle 3 \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}_4$, so the quotient is $\mathbb{Z}_4$.

knowledge_points.constraints: statement, well-definedness, injectivity, surjectivity — one step at a time

exemplars.answer: For a homomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$, the map $\bar\varphi : G/\ker\varphi \to \mathrm{im}\,\varphi$, $\bar\varphi(g\ker\varphi) = \varphi(g)$, is a well-defined isomorphism.
exemplars.problem: State the first isomorphism theorem and define the induced map.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Well defined because representatives differing by a kernel element have equal images; injective because the kernel collapses to the identity coset; surjective onto the image by construction.

exemplars.problem: In the proof, why is $\bar\varphi$ well defined?
exemplars.solution_sketch: Coset equality means the representatives differ by a kernel element, which $\varphi$ kills.

knowledge_points.name: Statement and the induced map

knowledge_points.constraints: quotients of Z, Z_n, S_n, D_n realized by reduction, sign, or power maps

exemplars.answer: Reduction $\varphi:\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_6$ is onto with kernel $6\mathbb{Z}$, so $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{Z}_6$.
exemplars.problem: Use the first isomorphism theorem to identify $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Pick the surjection whose kernel is the subgroup you are quotienting by.

exemplars.answer: $\mathrm{sgn}: S_4 \to \{\pm 1\}$ is onto with kernel $A_4$, so $S_4/A_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$.
exemplars.problem: Identify $S_4/A_4$ up to isomorphism using a homomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The sign map realizes the quotient as the two-element group.

knowledge_points.name: Identifying quotients via a good homomorphism

knowledge_points.constraints: existence/non-existence of surjections between groups of order <= 30

exemplars.problem: Prove that every homomorphic image of $G$ has order dividing $|G|$ (finite $G$).
exemplars.solution_sketch: First isomorphism theorem plus Lagrange.

exemplars.answer: The image would have order $3$, but $3 \nmid 8$.
exemplars.problem: Show there is no surjective homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}_8 \to \mathbb{Z}_3$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Image order divides domain order; $3$ does not divide $8$.

anki_seeds.back: P = h/k — and it is unstable: solutions diverge from it on both sides.
anki_seeds.front: Equilibrium of the harvested growth model P' = kP - h?
Terminal velocity for v' = g - (k/m)v?

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: A fish population grows at relative rate $0.4$ per year but is harvested at a constant $200$ fish per year: $P' = 0.4P - 200$. With $P(0) = 400$, when does the population die out? Give an exact answer.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: The equilibrium is $P = 500$, and $P = 500 + (400 - 500)e^{0.4t} = 500 - 100e^{0.4t}$. This is zero when $e^{0.4t} = 5$, i.e. $t = \frac{\ln 5}{0.4} = \frac{5\ln 5}{2}$.

knowledge_points.constraints: P' = kP - h with clean equilibrium h/k; the equilibrium is unstable — solutions diverge on both sides

exemplars.problem: A fish population grows at relative rate $0.5$/year but is harvested at $100$ fish/year: $P' = 0.5P - 100$. Find the equilibrium population.
Solve $P' = 0.5P - 100$ with $P(0) = 300$ and describe the long-run behavior.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $P - 200$ satisfies natural growth; starting above the (unstable) equilibrium, the population runs away upward.

exemplars.problem: Solve $P' = 0.5P - 100$ with $P(0) = 100$. When does the population die out?
exemplars.solution_sketch: Below the equilibrium the gap grows: $200 - 100e^{t/2} = 0$ gives $e^{t/2} = 2$.

knowledge_points.name: Growth with harvesting or immigration

knowledge_points.constraints: all models are y' = a - by with clean equilibrium a/b; emphasize the shared structure across contexts

exemplars.problem: A falling object obeys $v' = 10 - 2v$ with $v(0) = 0$ (drag proportional to speed). Find $v(t)$ and the terminal velocity.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Equilibrium $v = 5$; $v = 5 + Ce^{-2t}$ with $C = -5$.

exemplars.problem: A drug is infused at $20$ mg/h and eliminated at relative rate $1/4$ per hour: $A' = 20 - \dfrac{A}{4}$, $A(0) = 0$. Find $A(t)$ and the long-run amount.
A capacitor charges by $V' = \dfrac{12 - V}{2}$ with $V(0) = 0$. Find $V(t)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Same structure as a mixing tank: approach the source voltage $12$ exponentially.

knowledge_points.name: Linear models across domains

knowledge_points.constraints: first stage determines k from one measurement; second stage inverts for a time; answers exact in logarithms

exemplars.problem: Coffee at $90^{\circ}$C in a $20^{\circ}$C room cools to $70^{\circ}$C in $5$ minutes. How long after the start does it reach $50^{\circ}$C? Give an exact answer.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $T = 20 + 70e^{-kt}$; $T(5) = 70$ gives $e^{-5k} = \tfrac{5}{7}$. Then $70e^{-kt} = 30$ gives $t = \dfrac{\ln(7/3)}{k}$ with $k = \tfrac{1}{5}\ln\tfrac{7}{5}$.

exemplars.problem: A population doubles in $5$ hours. Exactly how long until it is $10$ times its initial size?
exemplars.solution_sketch: $k = \tfrac{\ln 2}{5}$; solve $e^{kt} = 10$.

knowledge_points.name: Two-stage prediction problems

anki_seeds.back: $f_x(a,b) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h,\,b) - f(a,\,b)}{h}$ — differentiate in $x$ holding $y = b$ fixed.
anki_seeds.front: Definition of the partial derivative $f_x(a, b)$ as a limit?
To compute $f_x$, treat {{c1::every other variable}} as a constant.

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Let $f(x, y, z) = \dfrac{xy}{x + z}$. Find $f_x$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Treat $y$ and $z$ as constants and use the quotient rule: $f_x = \dfrac{y(x + z) - xy}{(x + z)^2} = \dfrac{yz}{(x + z)^2}$.

knowledge_points.constraints: polynomial in x, y with integer coefficients, total degree at most 5

exemplars.problem: Let $f(x, y) = x^3 y^2 + 2x - y$. Find $f_x$ and $f_y$; state the pair $(f_x, f_y)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: For $f_x$ treat $y$ as a constant; for $f_y$ treat $x$ as a constant.

exemplars.problem: Let $f(x, y) = x^2 y^3$. Compute $f_y(1, 2)$.

knowledge_points.name: Partials of polynomials

knowledge_points.constraints: quadratic f so the difference quotient simplifies by cancellation; also test the equivalent notations for the partial derivative (∂z/∂x, ∂f/∂x, f_x) — never the straight-d dz/dx of one-variable calculus

exemplars.problem: For $f(x, y) = x^2 - 2xy$, use the limit definition to compute $f_x(1, 2)$.
Let $f(x, y) = x y^2$. Use the limit definition of $f_y$ (not the power rule) to compute $f_y(2, 1)$.

knowledge_points.name: The limit definition and notation

exemplars.problem: Let $f(x, y) = \dfrac{xy}{x + y}$. Find $f_x$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Quotient rule in $x$: $\frac{y(x+y) - xy}{(x+y)^2} = \frac{y^2}{(x+y)^2}$.

exemplars.problem: Let $f(x, y, z) = x^2 y + y z^3$. Find $f_z$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Both $x$ and $y$ are held constant; only the $yz^3$ term involves $z$.

anki_seeds.back: $k-1$ failure probabilities, then one success probability.
anki_seeds.front: P(first success on trial $k$) is built by multiplying...
P(first success within $k$ trials) $=$ ?

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Trials succeed independently with probability $1/4$. Find the probability that the first success comes within $2$ trials.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Complement of two straight failures: $1 - (3/4)^2 = 7/16$.

knowledge_points.constraints: exactly one failure before the success; p in {1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6}

exemplars.problem: A fair coin is flipped until heads. Find $P(\text{first head on flip } 2)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Tail then head: $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$.

exemplars.problem: A fair die is rolled until a $6$ appears. Find $P(\text{first } 6 \text{ on roll } 2)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: One failure then a success: $\frac{5}{6} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{36}$.

knowledge_points.name: Failure-then-success chains

knowledge_points.constraints: k <= 4; p in {1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6}; answers exact fractions

exemplars.problem: A fair die is rolled until a $6$ appears. Find $P(\text{first } 6 \text{ on roll } 3)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Two failures then a success: $\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{25}{216}$.

exemplars.problem: A fair coin is flipped until heads. Find $P(\text{first head on flip } 4)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{16}$.

knowledge_points.name: First success on trial k

knowledge_points.constraints: k <= 3; allow either summing cases or the all-failures complement

exemplars.problem: A fair coin is flipped until heads. Find $P(\text{first head within } 2 \text{ flips})$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$, or $1 - P(\text{both tails}) = 1 - \frac{1}{4}$.

exemplars.problem: Trials succeed with probability $1/3$. Find the probability the first success comes within two trials.

knowledge_points.name: First success within k trials

anki_seeds.back: The greatest integer $\le x$ (so $\lfloor x \rfloor \le x < \lfloor x \rfloor + 1$).
anki_seeds.front: Definition of $\lfloor x \rfloor$?
Definition of $\lceil x \rceil$?

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: $\lfloor -2.4 \rfloor = -3$ (the greatest integer not exceeding $-2.4$) and $\lceil 1.2 \rceil = 2$, so the sum is $-1$. And $\lceil x \rceil = 3$ exactly when $2 < x \le 3$, i.e. $x \in (2, 3]$: the least integer at or above $x$ equals $3$ precisely for those $x$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Compute $\lfloor -2.4 \rfloor + \lceil 1.2 \rceil$, and describe all real $x$ with $\lceil x \rceil = 3$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Round down for the floor (careful with negatives) and up for the ceiling; then read the ceiling condition as a half-open interval.

knowledge_points.constraints: evaluate at positives, negatives, and integers; negatives are the trap

exemplars.problem: Compute $\lfloor 3.7 \rfloor$, $\lceil 3.2 \rceil$, $\lfloor -1.5 \rfloor$, and $\lceil -2.3 \rceil$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Floor rounds down, ceiling rounds up: $\lfloor -1.5 \rfloor = -2$ since $-2 \le -1.5 < -1$, and $\lceil -2.3 \rceil = -2$ since $-3 < -2.3 \le -2$.

exemplars.problem: Compute $\lfloor 5 \rfloor$, $\lceil 5 \rceil$, and $\lfloor -0.5 \rfloor$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: On integers, floor and ceiling both return the integer itself; $-1 \le -0.5 < 0$ gives floor $-1$.

knowledge_points.name: Evaluating floor and ceiling

knowledge_points.constraints: verify a floor/ceiling identity at a concrete value

exemplars.problem: Verify $\lceil x \rceil = -\lfloor -x \rfloor$ at $x = 2.4$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\lceil 2.4 \rceil = 3$; and $-\lfloor -2.4 \rfloor = -(-3) = 3$.

exemplars.problem: Verify $\lfloor x + n \rfloor = \lfloor x \rfloor + n$ for $x = 1.5$, $n = 3$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\lfloor 4.5 \rfloor = 4$ and $\lfloor 1.5 \rfloor + 3 = 1 + 3 = 4$; integer shifts pass through the floor.

knowledge_points.name: Basic identities

knowledge_points.constraints: solution sets of $\lfloor x \rfloor = n$ or $\lceil x \rceil = n$ as intervals

exemplars.problem: Describe all real $x$ with $\lfloor x \rfloor = 4$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Floor equals $4$ exactly when $x$ lies in the half-open interval from $4$ up to but not including $5$.

exemplars.problem: Describe all real $x$ with $\lceil x \rceil = -1$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Ceiling equals $-1$ exactly when $x$ is at most $-1$ but greater than $-2$.

knowledge_points.name: Solving with floors and ceilings

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: A triangular plate has its base of $4$ m at the water surface and its apex $3$ m directly below the midpoint of the base. Find the fluid force on one side ($9800$ N/m$^3$).
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: The width at depth $y$ is $4(1 - y/3)$, so $F = 9800\int_0^3 y\cdot 4\left(1 - \frac{y}{3}\right)dy = 39200 \cdot \frac{3}{2}$.

knowledge_points.constraints: horizontal surfaces: force = pressure x area, no integral needed; weight density 9800 N/m^3

exemplars.problem: Water has weight density $9800$ N/m$^3$. Find the fluid force on the bottom of a pool $2$ m deep with bottom area $12$ m$^2$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Pressure at depth $2$ is $9800 \cdot 2 = 19600$ Pa; force $= 19600 \cdot 12 = 235200$ N.

exemplars.answer: $P = \rho g \, d$ (pressure grows linearly with depth)
exemplars.problem: State the fluid pressure at depth $d$ in a fluid of weight density $\rho g$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The weight of the fluid column of height $d$ over a unit area is $\rho g d$.

knowledge_points.name: Pressure and force on horizontal surfaces

knowledge_points.constraints: strips indexed by depth y; width constant; depths are small integers

exemplars.problem: A rectangular plate $2$ m wide is submerged vertically with its top edge $1$ m and bottom edge $3$ m below the surface. Find the fluid force on one side ($9800$ N/m$^3$).
exemplars.solution_sketch: A strip at depth $y$ has area $2\,dy$ and pressure $9800y$: $F = 9800\int_1^3 2y\,dy = 9800 \cdot 8 = 78400$ N.

exemplars.problem: A dam gate is a rectangle $3$ m wide whose top edge lies at the water surface and whose bottom edge is $2$ m deep. Find the force on the gate.

knowledge_points.name: Force on vertical rectangular plates

knowledge_points.constraints: width w(y) linear in depth, or the centroid shortcut for symmetric plates; state w(y) explicitly

exemplars.problem: A triangular plate has its base of $6$ m at the water surface and its apex $3$ m directly below the base's midpoint. Find the fluid force on one side ($9800$ N/m$^3$).
exemplars.solution_sketch: Width at depth $y$ is $6 - 2y$ (linear from $6$ to $0$): $F = 9800\int_0^3 y(6 - 2y)\,dy = 9800(27 - 18) = 88200$ N.

exemplars.problem: A circular plate of radius $1$ m is submerged vertically with its center $3$ m deep. Use the centroid shortcut $F = \rho g \bar{h} A$ to find the force.
exemplars.solution_sketch: By symmetry the average depth over the plate is the center's depth: $F = 9800 \cdot 3 \cdot \pi(1)^2 = 29400\pi$ N.

knowledge_points.name: Plates with varying width

anki_seeds.back: $\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}\, ds = \iint_D \operatorname{div}\mathbf{F}\, dA$, with $\mathbf{n}$ the outward normal.
anki_seeds.front: Flux (divergence) form of Green's theorem?

anki_seeds.back: Tangential form: circulation, via $Q_x - P_y$ (curl). Normal form: outward flux, via $P_x + Q_y$ (divergence).
anki_seeds.front: The two forms of Green's theorem measure what quantities?

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Use the flux form of Green's theorem to find the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle x^2 y,\; x y^2 \rangle$ across the boundary of the unit square $[0,1]^2$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = 2xy + 2xy = 4xy$, so the flux is $\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 4xy\,dx\,dy = 4\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2} = 1$.

knowledge_points.constraints: circles centered at the origin where n = <cos t, sin t>; F.n reduces via cos^2 or sin^2 averages

exemplars.problem: Compute the outward flux $\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}\, ds$ of $\mathbf{F} = \langle x, y \rangle$ across the unit circle.
exemplars.solution_sketch: On the unit circle the outward normal is $\langle \cos t, \sin t \rangle$ and $\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$; the flux is the arc length $2\pi$.

exemplars.problem: Compute the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle x, 0 \rangle$ across the unit circle.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} = \cos^2 t$; $\int_0^{2\pi} \cos^2 t\, dt = \pi$.

knowledge_points.name: Outward flux across a curve, directly

knowledge_points.constraints: div F is a constant or single monomial; regions are squares and origin-centered disks

exemplars.problem: Use the flux form of Green's theorem to find the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle x^2, y^2 \rangle$ across the boundary of the unit square $[0,1]^2$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = 2x + 2y$; flux $= \iint_{[0,1]^2} (2x + 2y)\, dA = 1 + 1 = 2$.

exemplars.problem: Find the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle x, y \rangle$ across the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 9$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = 2$, so the flux is $2 \cdot \text{area} = 2 \cdot 9\pi = 18\pi$.

exemplars.problem: Find the outward flux of $\mathbf{F} = \langle xy, y^2 \rangle$ across the boundary of the unit square $[0,1]^2$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = y + 2y = 3y$; $\iint 3y\, dA = \frac{3}{2}$.

exemplars.problem: Find the Fourier coefficients $b_n$ of $f(x) = x$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, using $b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin nx\,dx$.

exemplars.problem: The Fourier series of $f(x) = x$ on $(-\pi,\pi)$ is $\sum_{n\ge 1} \frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin nx$. Evaluate both sides at $x = \pi/2$ to sum $1 - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} - \cdots$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\sin(n\pi/2)$ vanishes for even $n$ and alternates for odd $n$; the identity $\frac{\pi}{2} = 2(1 - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} - \cdots)$ follows.

exemplars.problem: To what value does the Fourier series of $f(x) = x$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$ converge at the endpoint $x = \pi$?
exemplars.solution_sketch: The periodic extension jumps from $\pi$ to $-\pi$ there; the series converges to the midpoint $0$.

anki_seeds.front: Free-forgetful adjunction pattern?
The free vector space on a set $X$ is {{c1::$k^{(X)}$, with basis $X$}}.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Left adjoint: the discrete-space functor. Every function from a discrete space is continuous (all subsets are open in the source), so $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Top}}(X_{\mathrm{disc}},Y)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(X,UY)$, natural in both variables: $\mathrm{disc}\dashv U$. Right adjoint: the indiscrete-space functor. Every function into an indiscrete space is continuous (only $\varnothing$ and the whole set are open in the target), so $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Top}}(X,Y_{\mathrm{ind}})\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(UX,Y)$: $U\dashv\mathrm{ind}$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Show that the forgetful functor $U\colon\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Set}$ has both a left adjoint and a right adjoint, exhibiting the two hom-set bijections.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Ask on which side continuity comes for free. Every map out of a discrete space is continuous, giving $\mathrm{disc}\dashv U$; every map into an indiscrete space is continuous, giving $U\dashv\mathrm{ind}$. Each observation is itself the hom-set bijection.

knowledge_points.constraints: Stay at the level of the general pattern: name the free functor, the forgetful functor and the direction of the adjunction, then describe the unit as the universal insertion of generators $\eta_X\colon X\to U(FX)$ or the counit as the evaluation $\varepsilon_A\colon F(UA)\to A$ of formal expressions; no concrete algebra is computed.

exemplars.answer: Free $\dashv$ Forgetful; unit $\eta_X\colon X\to U(FX)$ inserts generators and is universal.
exemplars.problem: State the general free-forgetful adjunction pattern and describe its unit.
exemplars.solution_sketch: For an algebraic category $\mathcal A$ with forgetful $U\colon\mathcal A\to\mathbf{Set}$, the free functor $F$ satisfies $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(FX,A)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(X,UA)$, so $F\dashv U$. The unit $\eta_X\colon X\to U(FX)$ inserts generators and is universal: every function $X\to UA$ extends uniquely to a homomorphism $FX\to A$.

exemplars.answer: $\varepsilon_A\colon F(UA)\to A$ evaluates formal expressions, exhibiting $A$ as a quotient of the free algebra on its own elements.
exemplars.problem: Describe the counit of a free-forgetful adjunction $F\dashv U$ and say what it expresses.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The counit $\varepsilon_A=\Phi^{-1}(1_{UA})\colon F(UA)\to A$ is the unique homomorphism extending the identity $UA\to UA$: it sends each formal generator $[a]$ (for $a\in UA$) to $a$ and thereby evaluates formal expressions in $A$. It is surjective, so $A$ is a quotient of the free algebra $F(UA)$ on its underlying set — the canonical presentation by generators. The triangle identity $U\varepsilon\circ\eta U=1_U$ says evaluating an inserted generator returns it.

knowledge_points.name: The general pattern

knowledge_points.constraints: Free vector spaces $k^{(X)}$ on a set $X$ only; describe the free functor by its basis and every linear map out of it by its values on basis elements; a counit description must give the formula $\sum_v\lambda_v e_v\mapsto\sum_v\lambda_v v$ and say what presentation of $V$ it exhibits.

exemplars.answer: Free$(X)=k^{(X)}$, the space with basis $X$; linear maps out are free choices on the basis.
exemplars.problem: Instantiate free-forgetful for $U\colon\mathbf{Vect}_k\to\mathbf{Set}$ and describe the free functor.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $U$ forgets a vector space to its underlying set. The free functor sends $X$ to $k^{(X)}$, the finitely-supported functions $X\to k$ (formal linear combinations of $X$). A linear map $k^{(X)}\to V$ is freely determined by its values on the basis $X$, giving $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Vect}}(k^{(X)},V)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(X,UV)$. So Free $\dashv U$; the unit sends $x$ to the basis vector $e_x$.

exemplars.answer: $\varepsilon_V\colon k^{(UV)}\to V$, $\sum_v\lambda_v e_v\mapsto\sum_v\lambda_v v$; surjective, presenting $V\cong k^{(UV)}/\ker\varepsilon_V$.
exemplars.problem: Describe the counit of the free-forgetful adjunction for $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ at a space $V$ and interpret it.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The counit $\varepsilon_V=\Phi^{-1}(1_{UV})\colon k^{(UV)}\to V$ sends the basis vector $e_v$ (for $v\in UV$) to $v$, extending linearly: $\sum_v\lambda_v e_v\mapsto\sum_v\lambda_v v$. It is surjective since every vector is a linear combination of vectors, and its kernel is the subspace of all linear relations holding in $V$. Thus $V\cong k^{(UV)}/\ker\varepsilon_V$ presents $V$ by generators (its elements) and relations.

knowledge_points.name: Free vector spaces

knowledge_points.constraints: Forgetful functors carrying adjoints on both sides, limited to $U\colon\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Set}$ and $\mathrm{Ob}\colon\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{Set}$; the discrete construction must be identified as the LEFT adjoint and the indiscrete one as the RIGHT adjoint, each justified by saying which maps are automatically legal.

exemplars.answer: Discrete topology is left adjoint, indiscrete is right adjoint to $U$.
exemplars.problem: Explain why $U\colon\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Set}$ has both a left adjoint (discrete) and a right adjoint (indiscrete).
exemplars.solution_sketch: A continuous map from the discrete space $X_{\mathrm{disc}}$ to $Y$ is just any function $X\to UY$, so $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Top}}(X_{\mathrm{disc}},Y)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(X,UY)$: discrete $\dashv U$. Dually, a continuous map into the indiscrete space $Y_{\mathrm{ind}}$ is any function, so $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Top}}(X,Y_{\mathrm{ind}})\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(UX,Y)$: $U\dashv$ indiscrete. So $U$ has adjoints on both sides.

exemplars.problem: Show the object-set functor $\mathrm{Ob}\colon\mathbf{Cat}\to\mathbf{Set}$ has both a left adjoint (discrete category) and a right adjoint (indiscrete category).
exemplars.solution_sketch: A functor from the discrete category $\mathrm{disc}(S)$ (only identity arrows) to $\mathcal C$ is just a function $S\to\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal C)$, so $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Cat}}(\mathrm{disc}\,S,\mathcal C)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(S,\mathrm{Ob}\,\mathcal C)$: $\mathrm{disc}\dashv\mathrm{Ob}$. A functor into the indiscrete category $\mathrm{indisc}(S)$ (exactly one arrow between any two objects) is freely determined by its action on objects, so $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Cat}}(\mathcal C,\mathrm{indisc}\,S)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(\mathrm{Ob}\,\mathcal C,S)$: $\mathrm{Ob}\dashv\mathrm{indisc}$. Hence $\mathrm{Ob}$ has adjoints on both sides.

knowledge_points.name: A forgetful functor with adjoints on both sides

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: How many homomorphisms are there from the free group $F(\{a, b\})$ to $\mathbb{Z}_3$, and which group does the presentation $\langle x \mid x^5 = e \rangle$ define?
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Generators of a free group map freely; a single generator with $x^5 = e$ gives the cyclic group of order $5$.

knowledge_points.constraints: words of length <= 8 on at most 2 generators; note F on >= 2 generators is nonabelian (ab and ba are distinct reduced words)

exemplars.problem: In the free group $F(\{a, b\})$, reduce the word $a\,b\,b^{-1}\,a^{-1}\,b\,a$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Cancel adjacent inverse pairs: $a(bb^{-1})a^{-1}ba = (aa^{-1})ba = ba$; no further cancellation is possible.

exemplars.problem: Identify the free group on one generator, $F(\{a\})$, up to isomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Reduced words are exactly the powers $a^n$ ($n \in \mathbb{Z}$), and $a^m a^n = a^{m+n}$: the map $a^n \mapsto n$ is an isomorphism.

knowledge_points.name: Free groups and reduced words

knowledge_points.constraints: hom counts |G|^(number of generators) with |G| <= 8; contrast with the constrained counts for Z_m -> Z_n

exemplars.answer: Freeness: any choice $\varphi(a) = g$ extends uniquely by $\varphi(a^n) = g^n$, and there are no relations to respect — so $\varphi \leftrightarrow \varphi(a)$ is a bijection with $G$.
exemplars.problem: Explain why homomorphisms $F(\{a\}) \to G$ correspond exactly to elements of $G$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A homomorphism out of a free group is determined by, and free to choose, the images of the generators.

exemplars.problem: How many homomorphisms are there from $F(\{a, b\})$ to $\mathbb{Z}_5$?
exemplars.solution_sketch: Each of $a, b$ may map to any of the $5$ elements independently: $5^2 = 25$.

knowledge_points.name: The universal property: generators map freely

knowledge_points.constraints: match presentations to Z_n, D_n (n <= 6), and Z_m x Z_n (via commuting generators); target orders <= 12; that the relations cap the order may be quoted

exemplars.problem: Identify the group $\langle a \mid a^6 = e \rangle$ up to isomorphism.
exemplars.solution_sketch: One generator with the single relation $a^6 = e$ leaves exactly the powers $e, a, \dots, a^5$ — the cyclic group of order $6$ (the quotient of $F(\{a\})$ by the relation).

exemplars.problem: The presentation $\langle r, s \mid r^4 = s^2 = e,\ srs = r^{-1} \rangle$ defines which familiar group of order $8$?
exemplars.solution_sketch: These are exactly the dihedral relations: a quarter-turn $r$, a reflection $s$, and conjugation by $s$ inverting $r$; the relations reduce every word to one of $r^i s^j$ ($0 \le i < 4$, $j \in \{0,1\}$).

knowledge_points.name: Presentations by generators and relations

anki_seeds.front: Natural frequency of the undamped oscillator mx'' + kx = 0?
Amplitude of $x = a\cos\omega t + b\sin\omega t$?

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: A mass satisfies $x'' + 9x = 0$ with $x(0) = 3$ and $x'(0) = -12$. Solve the initial value problem and find the amplitude of the motion.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: The natural frequency is $\omega = 3$, so $x = c_1\cos 3t + c_2\sin 3t$ with $c_1 = 3$ and $3c_2 = -12$, i.e. $c_2 = -4$. The amplitude is $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$.

knowledge_points.constraints: k/m a perfect square; report omega = sqrt(k/m) and period 2 pi / omega

exemplars.problem: A $2$ kg mass hangs on a spring with stiffness $k = 32$ N/m, no damping. Write the equation of motion and its general solution.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $mx'' + kx = 0$ gives $x'' + (k/m)x = 0$ with $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{16} = 4$.

exemplars.problem: For $x'' + 25x = 0$, state the natural frequency and the period.
A $1$ kg mass on a spring with $k = 9$ N/m oscillates freely. What is the period?
exemplars.solution_sketch: $\omega = \sqrt{9/1} = 3$; $T = 2\pi/\omega$.

knowledge_points.name: The equation of motion

knowledge_points.constraints: initial data chosen so c_1, c_2 are small integers; x'(0) fixes c_2 through the factor omega

exemplars.solution_sketch: $x = c_1\cos 4t + c_2 \sin 4t$; the initial conditions give $c_1 = 3$, $c_2 = 0$.
$x(0) = 0$ kills the cosine and $x'(0) = 2c_2 = 6$ gives $c_2 = 3$.

knowledge_points.name: Oscillation IVPs

knowledge_points.constraints: amplitudes from Pythagorean pairs (3,4,5), (6,8,10), (1,sqrt3,2); phase angles at standard unit-circle values

exemplars.problem: A mass oscillates as $x = 3\cos 2t + 4\sin 2t$. Find the amplitude of the motion.
Write $x = \cos t + \sqrt{3}\sin t$ in the form $R\cos(t - \varphi)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $R = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2$; $\tan\varphi = \dfrac{b}{a} = \sqrt{3}$ with $a, b > 0$ gives $\varphi = \pi/3$.

exemplars.problem: Find the amplitude of $x = 6\cos t + 8\sin t$.

exemplars.solution_sketch: The total count is the sum of the frequencies: $4 + 7 + 9 = 20$.

anki_seeds.front: A functor is faithful when each hom-set map $\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(FA,FB)$ is...
A functor is full when each hom-set map $\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(FA,FB)$ is...
A fully faithful functor {{c1::reflects isomorphisms}} (if $Ff$ is iso then $f$ is iso).

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Let $Ff\colon FA\to FB$ have inverse $g\colon FB\to FA$. By fullness $g=Fh$ for some $h\colon B\to A$. Then $F(h\circ f)=Fh\circ Ff=g\circ Ff=1_{FA}=F(1_A)$, so faithfulness gives $h\circ f=1_A$. Symmetrically $F(f\circ h)=Ff\circ Fh=1_{FB}=F(1_B)$ gives $f\circ h=1_B$. Hence $h$ is a two-sided inverse and $f$ is an isomorphism.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Prove that a fully faithful functor $F$ reflects isomorphisms: if $Ff$ is an isomorphism, then $f$ is an isomorphism.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Fullness supplies the candidate and faithfulness proves it works: lift the inverse of $Ff$ to some $h\colon B\to A$, then descend the two identity equations from $\mathcal D$ to $\mathcal C$ by cancelling $F$.

knowledge_points.constraints: Phrase everything through the hom-set maps $F_{A,B}$; closure proofs (composites of faithful/full functors) factor $(GF)_{A,B}$ through the two hom-set maps.

exemplars.answer: Faithful: each $F_{A,B}$ injective; full: surjective; fully faithful: bijective.
exemplars.problem: Define faithful, full, and fully faithful in terms of the maps $F_{A,B}\colon\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(FA,FB)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A functor $F$ induces, for each pair $A,B$, a function $F_{A,B}\colon\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal D}(FA,FB)$, $f\mapsto Ff$. $F$ is faithful if every $F_{A,B}$ is injective, full if every $F_{A,B}$ is surjective, and fully faithful if every $F_{A,B}$ is a bijection. These conditions are about morphisms only; a faithful functor may still identify distinct objects.

exemplars.answer: A composite of injective hom-set maps is injective.
exemplars.problem: Using the hom-set formulation, prove that a composite of faithful functors is faithful.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $G\colon\mathcal D\to\mathcal E$ be faithful. For objects $A,B$ the map $(GF)_{A,B}\colon\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Hom}(GFA,GFB)$ factors as $G_{FA,FB}\circ F_{A,B}$. Each factor is injective by faithfulness of $F$ and of $G$, and a composite of injections is injective, so $(GF)_{A,B}$ is injective for all $A,B$. Hence $G\circ F$ is faithful.

knowledge_points.name: Definitions via the action on hom-sets

knowledge_points.constraints: Each judgment needs a witness: a non-homomorphism function for 'not full', a collapsed pair of morphisms for 'not faithful'; standard sources are forgetful functors and functors into $\mathbf 1$.

exemplars.answer: Distinct homomorphisms have distinct underlying functions; not every function is a homomorphism.
exemplars.problem: Show the forgetful functor $U\colon\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is faithful but not full.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Faithful: if $U\phi=U\psi$ as functions then $\phi=\psi$ as homomorphisms, so $U_{G,H}$ is injective. Not full: take $G=H=\mathbb Z$; the set function $n\mapsto n+1$ lies in $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z)$ but is not a group homomorphism (it does not fix $0$), so $U_{G,H}$ is not surjective.

exemplars.answer: Take $F\colon BM\to\mathbf 1$ for a monoid $M$ with $|M|\ge 2$ (say $M=\mathbb Z/2$); in general $\mathcal C\to\mathbf 1$ is full only when no hom-set of $\mathcal C$ is empty.
exemplars.problem: Give a functor that is full but not faithful, and explain why the unique functor $\mathcal C\to\mathbf 1$ is not full for every $\mathcal C$.
exemplars.solution_sketch:
Let $\mathbf 1$ have one object $*$ and only its identity, and let $F\colon\mathcal C	o\mathbf 1$ be the unique functor. Fullness asks each $F_{A,B}\colon\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)	o\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf 1}(*,*)=\{1_*\}$ to be surjective, which holds exactly when $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)
eq\varnothing$ — so $F$ fails to be full whenever some hom-set of $\mathcal C$ is empty (e.g. a discrete category on two objects). Choose instead $\mathcal C=BM$, the one-object category of a monoid $M$ with $|M|\ge 2$, such as $M=\mathbb Z/2$. It has a single object, so its only hom-set is $\mathrm{Hom}(*,*)=M
eq\varnothing$ and $F_{*,*}$ is surjective: $F$ is full. But $|M|\ge 2$ gives distinct parallel morphisms $m
eq n$ in $\mathrm{Hom}(*,*)$ with $Fm=1_*=Fn$, so $F_{*,*}$ is not injective and $F$ is not faithful.

knowledge_points.name: Examples that separate the notions

knowledge_points.constraints: The proof pattern is fixed: lift via fullness, verify via faithfulness; each application of fullness or faithfulness must be named where used.

exemplars.answer: Pull the inverse of $Ff$ back through fullness, then apply faithfulness.
exemplars.problem: Prove that a fully faithful functor $F$ reflects isomorphisms: if $Ff$ is an isomorphism, so is $f$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Suppose $Ff\colon FA\to FB$ has inverse $g\colon FB\to FA$. By fullness $g=Fh$ for some $h\colon B\to A$. Then $F(h\circ f)=Fh\circ Ff=g\circ Ff=1_{FA}=F(1_A)$; faithfulness gives $h\circ f=1_A$. Symmetrically $F(f\circ h)=Ff\circ Fh=1_{FB}=F(1_B)$ gives $f\circ h=1_B$. So $f$ is an isomorphism with inverse $h$.

exemplars.answer: Lift the iso and its inverse through fullness; faithfulness makes them mutually inverse.
exemplars.problem: Prove that if $F$ is fully faithful and $FA\cong FB$, then $A\cong B$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $\alpha\colon FA\to FB$ be an isomorphism with inverse $\beta\colon FB\to FA$. By fullness $\alpha=Ff$ and $\beta=Fg$ for some $f\colon A\to B$ and $g\colon B\to A$. Then $F(g\circ f)=Fg\circ Ff=\beta\circ\alpha=1_{FA}=F(1_A)$, and faithfulness gives $g\circ f=1_A$; symmetrically $f\circ g=1_B$. So $f$ is an isomorphism $A\cong B$.

knowledge_points.name: Fully faithful functors reflect isomorphisms

anki_seeds.front: In general, f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are...

diagnostic_exemplar.problem: If $f(x) = x + 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 3$, find $g(f(x))$.

knowledge_points.constraints: both rules linear with small integer coefficients; the answer is linear

exemplars.problem: If $f(x) = x + 1$ and $g(x) = 2x$, find $f(g(x))$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Substitute $g(x) = 2x$ into $f$: $2x + 1$.

exemplars.problem: If $f(x) = 3x$ and $g(x) = x - 2$, find $f(g(x))$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Substitute $g(x) = x - 2$ into $f$: $3(x - 2) = 3x - 6$.

exemplars.problem: Let $f(x)=x-3$ and $g(x)=x+3$. Simplify $f(g(x))$ and show how the translations cancel.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The composition is $(x+3)-3$. Adding and subtracting the same constant returns $x$.

exemplars.problem: A measurement converter doubles the input, $f(x)=2x$, then calibration adds five, $g(x)=x+5$. Write the complete conversion rule $g(f(x))$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The intermediate reading is $2x$. Calibration acts on that reading, so the final rule is $2x+5$.

knowledge_points.name: Symbolic composition of linear functions

knowledge_points.constraints: one rule is a squaring rule; expand the resulting perfect-square trinomial

exemplars.problem: If $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = x + 3$, find $f(g(x))$.
If $f(x) = 2x - 1$ and $g(x) = x^2$, find $g(f(x))$.
A square has side rule $g(x)=x-2$ and area rule $f(s)=s^2$. Expand the composition $f(g(x))$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The area uses the whole side length: $(x-2)(x-2)$. Expanding gives $x^2-2x-2x+4=x^2-4x+4$.

exemplars.problem: For $f(x)=3x+1$ and $g(x)=x^2$, a student writes $g(f(x))=3x^2+1$. Correct the composition and expand it.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The proposed expression reverses the order. The correct outer square is $(3x+1)^2$, whose terms are $9x^2$, $6x$, and $1$.

knowledge_points.name: Composition with squaring

knowledge_points.constraints: both rules linear; ask the same pair in both orders so that f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) differ

exemplars.problem: If $f(x) = x - 4$ and $g(x) = 3x + 1$, find $g(f(x))$.
If $f(x) = x - 4$ and $g(x) = 3x + 1$, find $f(g(x))$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $(3x + 1) - 4 = 3x - 3$; note it differs from $g(f(x))$.

exemplars.problem: Follow the symbolic pipeline $x\xrightarrow{g}x-5\xrightarrow{f}2(x-5)+3$, where $f(x)=2x+3$ and $g(x)=x-5$. Give its simplified output rule.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The diagram applies $g$ first. Distributing in $2(x-5)+3$ gives $2x-10+3=2x-7$.

exemplars.problem: A calibration pipeline first uses $f(x)=2x+3$, then uses $g(x)=x-5$. Give the rule for the final calibrated reading.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The second stage subtracts $5$ from the first-stage reading $2x+3$, giving $(2x+3)-5=2x-2$.

knowledge_points.name: Order matters (g(f(x)) vs f(g(x)))

anki_seeds.back: $g(f(x))$: apply $f$ first, then $g$ (requires codomain of $f$ = domain of $g$).
anki_seeds.front: Definition of the composition $(g \circ f)(x)$?
A function is invertible if and only if it is...

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: First, $g \circ f$ is a bijection: it is injective, since $g(f(a_1)) = g(f(a_2))$ gives $f(a_1) = f(a_2)$ by injectivity of $g$ and then $a_1 = a_2$ by injectivity of $f$; and surjective, since for $c \in C$ we may pick $b$ with $g(b) = c$ and then $a$ with $f(a) = b$. So it has a two-sided inverse. Now $(f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}) \circ (g \circ f) = f^{-1} \circ (g^{-1} \circ g) \circ f = f^{-1} \circ \mathrm{id}_B \circ f = \mathrm{id}_A$, and likewise $(g \circ f) \circ (f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}) = g \circ (f \circ f^{-1}) \circ g^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_C$. A two-sided inverse is unique, so $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: For bijections $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$, prove that $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Check that $g \circ f$ is a bijection, then verify $f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ composes with it to the identity on both sides and appeal to uniqueness of inverses.

knowledge_points.constraints: peel off $g$ then $f$ using each map''s injectivity

exemplars.problem: Prove: if $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$ are both injective, then $g \circ f$ is injective.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Assume $(g \circ f)(a_1) = (g \circ f)(a_2)$, i.e. $g(f(a_1)) = g(f(a_2))$. Injectivity of $g$ gives $f(a_1) = f(a_2)$; injectivity of $f$ gives $a_1 = a_2$. So $g \circ f$ is injective. $\square$

exemplars.problem: Prove: if $g \circ f$ is injective, then $f$ is injective.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Suppose $f(a_1) = f(a_2)$. Applying $g$ gives $(g \circ f)(a_1) = (g \circ f)(a_2)$, and injectivity of $g \circ f$ forces $a_1 = a_2$. (Note $g$ itself need not be injective.) $\square$

knowledge_points.name: Composition preserves injectivity

knowledge_points.constraints: use surjectivity for existence and injectivity for uniqueness of the inverse

exemplars.answer: Define $f^{-1}(b)$ as the unique preimage; check both compositions are identities.
exemplars.problem: Prove: if $f : A \to B$ is bijective then it has a two-sided inverse $f^{-1} : B \to A$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Surjectivity gives, for each $b$, some $a$ with $f(a) = b$; injectivity makes it unique, so $f^{-1}(b) = a$ is well-defined. Then $f(f^{-1}(b)) = b$ and $f^{-1}(f(a)) = a$, so $f^{-1}$ is a two-sided inverse. $\square$

exemplars.problem: Find the inverse of $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = 2x + 3$, and verify it.

knowledge_points.name: Inverses and bijections

knowledge_points.constraints: verify a candidate inverse by composing both ways

exemplars.answer: Composition with $g \circ f$ gives the identities.
exemplars.problem: For bijections $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to C$, prove $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: $(f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}) \circ (g \circ f) = f^{-1} \circ (g^{-1} \circ g) \circ f = f^{-1} \circ f = \mathrm{id}_A$, and similarly the other order gives $\mathrm{id}_C$. By uniqueness of inverses, $(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$. $\square$

anki_seeds.front: The functor category $[\mathcal C,\mathcal D]$ has objects ___ and morphisms ___.
An isomorphism in a functor category is exactly a {{c1::natural isomorphism}}.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: A functor $F\colon\mathbf BG\to\mathbf{Set}$ is a set $X=F(*)$ together with the maps $g\cdot x:=F(g)(x)$; the functor laws say $1\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$, i.e. a $G$-action. A natural transformation $\alpha\colon F\Rightarrow F'$ has a single component $\alpha_*\colon X\to X'$, and the naturality square at $g\in G$ reads $\alpha_*(g\cdot x)=g\cdot\alpha_*(x)$: natural transformations are exactly the $G$-equivariant maps. ($\Rightarrow$) If $\alpha$ is invertible in $[\mathbf BG,\mathbf{Set}]$ there is $\beta$ with $\beta\cdot\alpha=1_F$ and $\alpha\cdot\beta=1_{F'}$; vertical composition and identities are componentwise, so $\beta_*$ is a two-sided inverse of $\alpha_*$ and $\alpha_*$ is a bijection. ($\Leftarrow$) If $\alpha_*$ is a bijection, put $y=\alpha_*(x)$ in $\alpha_*(g\cdot x)=g\cdot\alpha_*(x)$ and apply $\alpha_*^{-1}$: $\alpha_*^{-1}(g\cdot y)=g\cdot\alpha_*^{-1}(y)$, so $\alpha_*^{-1}$ is equivariant and therefore a natural transformation $F'\Rightarrow F$; componentwise it is a two-sided inverse of $\alpha$. Hence the isomorphisms of $[\mathbf BG,\mathbf{Set}]$ are exactly the equivariant bijections.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Let $\mathbf BG$ be the one-object category of a group $G$, so that functors $\mathbf BG\to\mathbf{Set}$ are $G$-sets. Describe the natural transformations between two such functors, and prove that a transformation $\alpha\colon F\Rightarrow F'$ is an isomorphism of the functor category $[\mathbf BG,\mathbf{Set}]$ if and only if its single component is a bijection.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: First translate: a functor $\mathbf BG\to\mathbf{Set}$ is a $G$-set, and the single naturality square reads $\alpha_*(g\cdot x)=g\cdot\alpha_*(x)$, so transformations are exactly the equivariant maps. Then use that composition in a functor category is componentwise, and check that the set-theoretic inverse of an equivariant bijection is again equivariant.

knowledge_points.constraints: Verify the category axioms componentwise in $\mathcal D$; structural transfer results (e.g. groupoid target gives groupoid functor category) must construct the inverse transformation explicitly.

exemplars.answer: Objects: functors $\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$; morphisms: natural transformations; composition vertical; identity $(1_F)_A=1_{FA}$.
exemplars.problem: Define the functor category $[\mathcal C,\mathcal D]$ and verify it is a category.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Objects are functors $F\colon\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$; a morphism $F\to G$ is a natural transformation $\alpha\colon F\Rightarrow G$; composition is vertical composition $(\beta\alpha)_A=\beta_A\circ\alpha_A$, which is natural; the identity on $F$ has components $1_{FA}$. Associativity and the unit laws hold componentwise because they hold in $\mathcal D$, so $[\mathcal C,\mathcal D]$ is a category.

exemplars.answer: Every component is iso, so every natural transformation is invertible.
exemplars.problem: Prove that if $\mathcal D$ is a groupoid then the functor category $[\mathcal C,\mathcal D]$ is also a groupoid.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Let $\alpha\colon F\Rightarrow G$ be any morphism of $[\mathcal C,\mathcal D]$. Each component $\alpha_A\colon FA\to GA$ is a morphism of the groupoid $\mathcal D$, hence an isomorphism. Since every component is iso, the componentwise inverses $\alpha_A^{-1}$ assemble into a natural transformation $G\Rightarrow F$ that is a two-sided inverse of $\alpha$ in $[\mathcal C,\mathcal D]$. Thus every morphism is invertible, i.e. $[\mathcal C,\mathcal D]$ is a groupoid.
