anki_seeds.front: The Yoneda embedding $\mathbf{y}\colon\mathcal C\to[\mathcal C^{op},\mathbf{Set}]$ sends $A\mapsto$? and $f\mapsto$?
What key property does the Yoneda embedding have?
A fully faithful embedding lets you conclude $A\cong B$ from {{c1::$\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$}}.

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: The maps $f_*$ are exactly the components of $\mathbf y(f)=f\circ(-)\colon\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$, the image of $f$ under the Yoneda embedding $\mathbf y\colon\mathbf{Grp}\to[\mathbf{Grp}^{op},\mathbf{Set}]$; the hypothesis says every component is a bijection, i.e. $\mathbf y(f)$ is a natural isomorphism. Since $\mathbf y$ is fully faithful and fully faithful functors reflect isomorphisms, $f$ is an isomorphism. Directly: take $X=B$; surjectivity of $f_*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(B,A)\to\mathrm{Hom}(B,B)$ gives $g\colon B\to A$ with $f\circ g=1_B$. Then, in $\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$, $f\circ(g\circ f)=(f\circ g)\circ f=f=f\circ 1_A$, and injectivity of $f_*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(A,A)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$ gives $g\circ f=1_A$. So $g$ is a two-sided inverse and $f$ is an isomorphism.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Let $f\colon A\to B$ be a homomorphism of groups such that for every group $X$ the map $f_*\colon\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}}(X,A)\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}}(X,B)$, $h\mapsto f\circ h$, is a bijection. Prove that $f$ is an isomorphism, and identify the natural transformation whose components the maps $f_*$ are.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Recognise the family $f_*$ as the components of $\mathbf y(f)$, so the hypothesis says $\mathbf y(f)$ is a natural isomorphism; $\mathbf y$ is fully faithful and therefore reflects isomorphisms. Concretely the same conclusion comes from taking $X=B$ to produce the inverse and $X=A$ to force the other identity.

knowledge_points.constraints: Define $\mathbf y$ on objects and on morphisms and say which composition it uses (post-composition for the presheaf version, pre-composition for the covariant-hom version, which is contravariant on $\mathcal C$); functoriality is a one-line check of each law.

exemplars.problem: Define the Yoneda embedding $\mathbf{y}\colon\mathcal C\to[\mathcal C^{op},\mathbf{Set}]$ and confirm it is a functor.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The Yoneda embedding sends $A$ to the representable presheaf $\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)$ and $f\colon A\to B$ to the natural transformation $f_*=f\circ(-)\colon\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$. Functoriality holds because $(g f)_*=g_*\circ f_*$ and $(1_A)_*=1$; each $f_*$ is natural since post- and pre-composition commute by associativity.

exemplars.problem: Describe the covariant-hom embedding $A\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ into $[\mathcal C,\mathbf{Set}]$ and confirm it is functorial (contravariant on $\mathcal C$).
exemplars.solution_sketch: Send each object $A$ to $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ and each $f\colon A\to B$ to $f^*=(-)\circ f$, the natural transformation with component $\mathrm{Hom}(B,X)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,X)$, $g\mapsto g\circ f$. Each $f^*$ is natural since pre- and post-composition commute. Because $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$ and $(1_A)^*=1$, the assignment is a contravariant functor $\mathcal C\to[\mathcal C,\mathbf{Set}]$, i.e. a functor $\mathcal C^{op}\to[\mathcal C,\mathbf{Set}]$.

knowledge_points.name: The embedding as a functor

knowledge_points.constraints: Two routes only: quote the contravariant Yoneda lemma at a second representable, or argue directly by evaluating at identities ($f_*(1_A)=f$ for faithfulness, $\theta=\big(\theta_A(1_A)\big)_*$ for fullness); name which of full and faithful each step establishes.

exemplars.answer: The contravariant Yoneda lemma gives $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathbf{y}A,\mathbf{y}B)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$, and the bijection is $f\mapsto f_*$.
exemplars.problem: Prove the Yoneda embedding is fully faithful.
exemplars.solution_sketch: By the contravariant Yoneda lemma, $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,A),\mathrm{Hom}(-,B))\cong\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$, and unwinding the bijection shows the transformation corresponding to $f$ is exactly $f_*=\mathbf{y}(f)$. Hence $\mathbf{y}_{A,B}\colon\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)\to\mathrm{Nat}(\mathbf{y}A,\mathbf{y}B)$ is a bijection, so $\mathbf{y}$ is fully faithful.

exemplars.problem: Give a direct proof, evaluating at identities, that $\mathbf{y}$ is both faithful and full.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Faithful: if $f_*=g_*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$, evaluate components at $1_A\in\mathrm{Hom}(A,A)$ to get $f=f_*(1_A)=g_*(1_A)=g$. Full: given natural $\theta\colon\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$, set $f=\theta_A(1_A)$; naturality of $\theta$ at any $h\colon X\to A$ applied to $1_A$ gives $\theta_X(h)=\theta_X(1_A\circ h)=f\circ h=f_*(h)$, so $\theta=f_*=\mathbf{y}(f)$. Hence $\mathbf{y}$ is fully faithful.

knowledge_points.name: Full faithfulness

knowledge_points.constraints: Consequences of full faithfulness — reflection of isomorphisms, objects determined by their points; every step must cite full faithfulness or the naturality of $\mathbf y(f)$, and a hypothesis quantified over all objects $X$ must be instantiated at a specific $X$ (typically $X=A$ or $X=B$).

exemplars.answer: Fully faithful functors reflect isomorphisms; $\mathcal C$ is a full subcategory of $[\mathcal C^{op},\mathbf{Set}]$.
exemplars.problem: Explain why $A\cong B$ iff $\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$, and why $\mathcal C$ embeds into presheaves.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A fully faithful functor reflects isomorphisms, so $\mathbf{y}A\cong\mathbf{y}B$ implies $A\cong B$; functors always preserve isos, giving the converse. Thus an object is determined up to isomorphism by its presheaf of points $\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)$. Since $\mathbf{y}$ is fully faithful, it identifies $\mathcal C$ with a full subcategory of the presheaf category $[\mathcal C^{op},\mathbf{Set}]$ — every category is (equivalent to) a category of structured sets and maps.

exemplars.answer: $f$ iso $\iff\mathbf{y}(f)$ a natural iso $\iff$ each component $f_*$ is a bijection.

exemplars.solution_sketch: $\mathbf{y}$ is fully faithful, hence reflects isomorphisms: $f$ is an iso iff $\mathbf{y}(f)=f_*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$ is an isomorphism of presheaves. A natural transformation of $\mathbf{Set}$-valued functors is an isomorphism iff each component is a bijection. So $f$ is an iso iff $f_*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(X,A)\to\mathrm{Hom}(X,B)$ is bijective for all $X$ — isomorphisms are detected on generalized elements.

anki_seeds.front: The Yoneda isomorphism is natural in which variables?

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: Inverse: for $u\in GA$ define $\Theta(u)_X\colon\mathrm{Hom}(X,A)\to GX$ by $\Theta(u)_X(h)=(Gh)(u)$. This is natural: for $k\colon W\to X$ the presheaf $\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)$ acts by pre-composition, and $\Theta(u)_W(h\circ k)=G(h\circ k)(u)=\big(Gk\circ Gh\big)(u)=Gk\big(\Theta(u)_X(h)\big)$, using the contravariant composition law $G(h\circ k)=Gk\circ Gh$. Round trip 1: $\Psi(\Theta(u))=\Theta(u)_A(1_A)=G(1_A)(u)=u$, since $G(1_A)=1_{GA}$. Round trip 2: for $\alpha$ natural and $h\colon X\to A$, naturality of $\alpha$ at $h$ reads $\alpha_X\circ(-\circ h)=Gh\circ\alpha_A$; evaluating both sides at $1_A$ gives $\alpha_X(h)=Gh(\alpha_A(1_A))=\Theta(\Psi(\alpha))_X(h)$, so $\Theta\Psi=\mathrm{id}$. Hence $\Psi$ is a bijection with inverse $\Theta$. Naturality in $G$: for $\varphi\colon G\Rightarrow G'$ the square compares $\alpha\mapsto\varphi\cdot\alpha\mapsto(\varphi\cdot\alpha)_A(1_A)=\varphi_A(\alpha_A(1_A))$ with $\alpha\mapsto\alpha_A(1_A)\mapsto\varphi_A(\alpha_A(1_A))$; the two routes agree, so the square commutes.
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Prove the contravariant Yoneda lemma: for a presheaf $G\colon\mathcal C^{op}\to\mathbf{Set}$ and an object $A$, the assignment $\Psi(\alpha)=\alpha_A(1_A)$ is a bijection $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,A),G)\to GA$. Exhibit the inverse, verify both round trips, and check that the bijection is natural in $G$.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: Both directions are a chase of the identity. $\Psi$ evaluates at $1_A$, and naturality of $\alpha$ at $h$ applied to $1_A$ forces $\alpha_X(h)=Gh(\alpha_A(1_A))$ — which is what the inverse $\Theta(u)_X(h)=(Gh)(u)$ must be. The other round trip is $G(1_A)=1_{GA}$, and naturality in $G$ is a one-line comparison of the two routes.

knowledge_points.constraints: Write both maps explicitly, $\Theta(u)_X(h)=(Fh)(u)$ and $\Psi(\alpha)=\alpha_A(1_A)$; naturality of $\Theta(u)$ must cite the composition law of $F$, and each round trip must cite either $F(1_A)=1_{FA}$ or naturality of $\alpha$ — one citation per step, no elements of $\mathcal C$.

exemplars.answer: Naturality at $k\colon X\to Y$ is the composition law $F(k\circ h)=Fk\circ Fh$.
exemplars.problem: Prove that $\Theta(u)$, defined by $\Theta(u)_X(h)=(Fh)(u)$ for $u\in FA$, really is a natural transformation $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)\Rightarrow F$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Fix $u\in FA$ and set $\Theta(u)_X\colon\mathrm{Hom}(A,X)\to FX$, $h\mapsto(Fh)(u)$; the type is right since $Fh\colon FA\to FX$. For $k\colon X\to Y$, naturality asks $Fk\circ\Theta(u)_X=\Theta(u)_Y\circ\mathrm{Hom}(A,k)$. On $h\in\mathrm{Hom}(A,X)$ the left side gives $Fk\big((Fh)(u)\big)=F(k\circ h)(u)$ by functoriality, and the right side gives $\Theta(u)_Y(k\circ h)=F(k\circ h)(u)$. They agree, so $\Theta(u)$ is natural.

exemplars.problem: Prove the two maps $\Psi(\alpha)=\alpha_A(1_A)$ and $\Theta(u)_X(h)=(Fh)(u)$ are mutually inverse.
exemplars.solution_sketch: First, $\Theta(u)$ is natural by functoriality of $F$. Then $\Psi(\Theta(u))=\Theta(u)_A(1_A)=(F1_A)(u)=u$, so $\Psi\Theta=\mathrm{id}$. Conversely, for any $\alpha$ and $h\colon A\to X$, naturality of $\alpha$ at $h$ applied to $1_A$ gives $\alpha_X(h)=\alpha_X(h\circ 1_A)=(Fh)(\alpha_A(1_A))=\Theta(\Psi(\alpha))_X(h)$, so $\Theta\Psi=\mathrm{id}$. Hence the correspondence is a bijection.

knowledge_points.constraints: Name the two induced maps forming the square, then evaluate both routes on a transformation $\alpha$.

exemplars.answer: For $\phi\colon F\Rightarrow F'$ both routes send $\alpha\mapsto\phi_A(\alpha_A(1_A))$, so the square commutes.
exemplars.problem: Prove that the Yoneda bijection $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(A,-),F)\cong FA$ is natural in $F$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Write $\Psi_F(\alpha)=\alpha_A(1_A)$. A natural transformation $\phi\colon F\Rightarrow F'$ induces post-composition $\phi\circ(-)$ on $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(A,-),-)$ and $\phi_A$ on evaluation at $A$. Then $\Psi_{F'}(\phi\circ\alpha)=(\phi\circ\alpha)_A(1_A)=\phi_A(\alpha_A(1_A))=\phi_A(\Psi_F(\alpha))$, so the naturality square commutes. Hence the Yoneda isomorphism is natural in $F$.

exemplars.problem: Prove that the Yoneda bijection is natural in $A$: for $f\colon A\to B$, pre-composing with $f^*\colon\mathrm{Hom}(B,-)\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ corresponds to applying $Ff$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: For $f\colon A\to B$ let $f^*$ have components $(f^*)_X(g)=g\circ f$, so $\alpha\mapsto\alpha\circ f^*$ maps $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(A,-),F)$ to $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(B,-),F)$; on the other side the map is $Ff\colon FA\to FB$. Route one: $\Psi_B(\alpha\circ f^*)=(\alpha\circ f^*)_B(1_B)=\alpha_B(1_B\circ f)=\alpha_B(f)$. Route two: $Ff\big(\Psi_A(\alpha)\big)=Ff\big(\alpha_A(1_A)\big)$, which by naturality of $\alpha$ at $f$ equals $\alpha_B(f\circ 1_A)=\alpha_B(f)$. The two agree, so the bijection is natural in $A$ as well.

exemplars.problem: State the contravariant Yoneda lemma and compute $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,A),\mathrm{Hom}(-,B))$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: For presheaves $G\colon\mathcal C^{op}\to\mathbf{Set}$, $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,A),G)\cong GA$ naturally. Taking $G=\mathrm{Hom}(-,B)$ yields $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,A),\mathrm{Hom}(-,B))\cong\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$: natural transformations between representables are exactly morphisms of the representing objects — the computational core of the Yoneda embedding.

exemplars.problem: Use the contravariant Yoneda lemma to compute the monoid of natural endomorphisms of the presheaf $\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)$.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Taking $G=\mathrm{Hom}(-,A)$ in $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,A),G)\cong GA$ gives $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,A),\mathrm{Hom}(-,A))\cong\mathrm{Hom}(A,A)=\mathrm{End}(A)$, with $\alpha\mapsto\alpha_A(1_A)$ and inverse $f\mapsto f_*=f\circ(-)$. Since $(g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*$ and $(1_A)_*=1$, the bijection respects composition and units, so it is an isomorphism of monoids.

anki_seeds.front: How many natural transformations $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)\Rightarrow F$ are there?

diagnostic_exemplar.answer: The action is well defined: sending $1$ to the transposition of $\{p,q\}$ extends to a homomorphism $\mathbb Z/4\to\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ because the transposition has order $2$, which divides $4$. Writing $*$ for the unique object, the representable presheaf is $\mathrm{Hom}(-,*)=M$ with right multiplication, and the contravariant Yoneda lemma gives $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,*),X)\cong X(*)=X$ via $\alpha\mapsto\alpha(e)$, where $e=0$ is the identity. Concretely the transformation attached to $x\in X$ is $\alpha^x(m)=x\cdot m$, which is equivariant since $(x\cdot m)\cdot m'=x\cdot(mm')$, and $\alpha^x(e)=x$ recovers $x$. So the equivariant maps $M\to X$ correspond bijectively to the elements of $X$, and there are exactly $2$ of them (namely $m\mapsto p\cdot m$ and $m\mapsto q\cdot m$).
diagnostic_exemplar.problem: Let $M=\mathbb Z/4$ (written additively) be viewed as a one-object category, so that presheaves on it are right $M$-sets. Use the Yoneda lemma to describe the natural transformations from the representable presheaf (the regular right $M$-set $M$) to $X$, and say exactly how many there are.
diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: First check the action is well defined: a transposition has order $2$, which divides $4$. Then apply Yoneda at the unique object, $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,*),X)\cong X$ by $\alpha\mapsto\alpha(e)$, so the equivariant maps are $m\mapsto x\cdot m$, one for each element $x$.

exemplars.problem: In $\mathbf{Set}$, count the natural transformations $\mathrm{Hom}(\{1,2\},-)\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}(\{1,2,3\},-)$, and count the natural transformations $\mathrm{Hom}(\{*\},-)\Rightarrow P$ where $P$ is the covariant power-set functor.

exemplars.answer: Presheaves on $BM$ are right $M$-sets; the representable one is $M$ acting on itself on the right.
exemplars.problem: For a monoid $M$, identify the presheaf category on $BM$ and describe the representable presheaf.
exemplars.solution_sketch: A presheaf $X\colon BM^{op}\to\mathbf{Set}$ picks a set $X(*)$ and, for each $m\in M$, a map $X(m)\colon X(*)\to X(*)$ with $X(mn)=X(n)\circ X(m)$ and $X(e)=\mathrm{id}$ — that is a right action $x\cdot m$. The representable presheaf $\mathrm{Hom}(-,*)$ has underlying set $\mathrm{Hom}(*,*)=M$, and a morphism $m$ acts by pre-composition $h\mapsto h\circ m=hm$: the right regular action of $M$ on itself.

diagnostic_exemplar.solution_sketch: $z_1 = (84 - 72)/6 = 2$ and $z_2 = (55 - 40)/10 = 1.5$; the first mark stands further above its own mean, so its z-score $2$ is the answer.

exemplars.problem: Test A (marked out of $10$) has mean $6$, SD $1$; test B has mean $7$, SD $1.5$. Which is relatively better: an $8$ on test A or an $8.5$ on test B? Give the z-score of the better one.
exemplars.solution_sketch: Test A: $z = (8-6)/1 = 2$. Test B: $z = (8.5-7)/1.5 = 1$. Higher z-score means further above its own mean.

exemplars.problem: Which is more unusual: $z = -2.5$ or $z = 1.8$? Give that z-score.

exemplars.solution_sketch: The factors give $x-3=0$ or $x+5=0$. Solving the linear equations gives $x=3$ or $x=-5$.

exemplars.problem: The graph $y=x(x-4)$ meets the horizontal axis where a factor vanishes. Find all corresponding $x$ values.
exemplars.solution_sketch: At an axis intersection the product is zero. The factors $x$ and $x-4$ give $x=0$ and $x=4$.

exemplars.problem: A student keeps only $x=6$ from $(x-6)(x+2)=0$. Give the complete solution set.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The second factor also can vanish: $x+2=0$ gives $-2$. Together with $x-6=0$, the full root set is $6,-2$.

exemplars.problem: A rectangular model has signed area $A=x(x+9)$. Find every real parameter $x$ for which this algebraic area is zero.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The area product vanishes at $x=0$ or $x+9=0$. Both are allowed real parameters, giving $0,-9$.

exemplars.problem: A student cancels $x$ in $x(x-3)(x+4)=0$ and loses a root. Give the complete solution set.
exemplars.solution_sketch: The factor $x$ contributes zero; cancelling it would lose that root. The other equations $x-3=0$ and $x+4=0$ give $3$ and $-4$.
